2. You learn concrete methods of practice.
3. It carries a mighty power of transformation.

blocks.text: Preface to the Complete Dream Wanderings Collection of Master Hanshan

inline.s: The Complete Dream Wanderings Collection of Master Hanshan was printed in the Jiaxing Canon in only five fascicles of recorded teachings. In the bing-shen year Gong Xiaosheng entered Guangdong, and the monk Huashou of Haizhuang obtained my letter; he struck the wooden clapper and announced it to the assembly, and sought out the manuscript kept by Chan Master Qixuan of Dinghu. Cao Qiuyue and the others had it copied and carried back to Wu, where Qian Qianyi personally collated it by hand and arranged it into forty fascicles. When the Master wrote, he finished as soon as his brush touched the paper, never pausing to amend; thus his phrases are sometimes redundant and his paragraphs occasionally out of order. On his journey east he once entrusted me with the preface to Master Zuo's Method of Mind for revision before publication; when he saw it he was delighted and struck out his earlier draft. In the collation I have now made, I have presumptuously altered a few strokes here and there; but this truly follows the Master's own parting words, and I would not dare to overstep and commit such an offense. When the work was complete I wrote this preface, saying: The Buddhas and patriarchs spread the teaching and spoke the Dharma by means of letters. Maitreya expounded the Yogacara, Nagarjuna interpreted the Prajna; a thousand gates and ten thousand doors, their nets of light crossing one another, rich and dense, brilliant and bright: the highest writing of a thousand ages. When the great teaching flowed eastward, humane letters gradually awakened. Dunsun and Huiyuan opened the way in the south, Kumarajiva and Sengzhao spread it wide in the north; the first cart and the great chariot truly began there. From the Sui and Tang onward, the writings of Tiantai, Qingliang, and Yongming were like the sun adorning the sky, like water running over the earth. Vast indeed were those fords of principle and that ocean-deep sea of letters. Down to the Song, the teaching grew broad and its writing grew tangled; three houses were the most eminent. Tanjin upheld the teaching with a lone loftiness, and his writing was spare and discriminating. Shimen supported the school with quick intelligence, and his writing was deep and lovely. Jingshan responded to capacities with generous breadth, and his writing was bright and unrestrained. Now when writing reaches discrimination, loveliness, and unrestraint, its ramparts grow daily firmer, its branches and leaves daily richer, and its gathering and drawing in of beings daily wider. Vast and overflowing, its words pour out like the rising sun; and perilously, the ford and bridge grow daily more weary. The Appended Remarks say: Was the making of the Yi not in the middle antiquity? Did he who made the Yi not have anxiety? How true this is. Our Master, of vast wisdom and deep compassion, truly practiced and truly awakened. The wisdom of mind-only he received in a dream from Maitreya; the Huayan dharma-realm he awakened to completely through Qingliang. Suiting capacities and answering illnesses, he spoke sideways and he spoke upright; a thousand sayings and ten thousand verses flowed one by one out of the Tathagata's ocean of letters. With the teaching-upheld stance of Tanjin he fortified his ramparts; with the school-supporting stance of Shimen he watered his branches and leaves; with the capacity-answering stance of Jingshan he gave free course to his gathering and drawing in. His one aim was to let the beings of the final age be touched by a single word or half a phrase, all to drink their fill from the river and return together to the ocean of wisdom, and only then to stop. The Flower Ornament says that the king of golden-winged birds, with pure eyes, surveys the dragons; those whose lives are due to end he strikes with his left and right wings, churning up the waters of the sea so that they part on both sides, and then takes and eats them. When the Master preached the Dharma for people, he wished to beat up the waters of the great sea of birth and death, seize beings of good roots, and set them within the Buddhadharma; and it was just so with him. Of late, the copyist Chen Fanghou of Guangnan, at a single phrase, sorrowfully awakened, cast down his brush, and shaved his head. The Master's seizing of his deep resolve blazed with radiance, and marvels burst forth from the paper. Beings of good roots breathe it in as their capacities allow; and men like Fanghou, through kalpas as many as the sands of the Ganges, will not yet be exhausted. How magnificent! The Master and Venerable Zibai both, with the stuff of heroes rarely born in any age, stood at the hour when the lion's string had fallen silent, and gave up body for the Dharma, one cart with two wheels. Zibai's writing is vigorous and decisive; the Master's writing is winding and tenderly mournful. But as a torch for the benighted road, they are one. People of old lamented that Zhongfeng laid down his mat and no one knew where Daoyin had gone; they said that after Chushi and Jitan the single branch of the flower held aloft had nearly died out. Looking from today, if it does not return to Zibai and Hanshan, to whom should it return? Five hundred years later the hosts of Mara and the outsiders rise like a sharpened edge, and these two craftsmen are born in answer, envoys of the Tathagata, wearing the great Dharma seal and kindling the great Dharma lamp: surely what the Confucians call worthies brought forth in due season for the age. The peddlers and plagiarists and thieves among them constantly usurp the lineage, attach themselves to a master's succession, and secretly shake the tree like mayflies. Yet once a master's collected works circulate, they are like the sun's disc at high noon; goblins and specters hide their shadows, and only the sleepwalker remains muddled and unawakened. And so the Master's great compassion of one body with all, like the anxiety of him who made the Yi, when will it ever cease? For this one may well weep aloud. When the Dream Wanderings Collection first circulated, the monk Juelang of Tianjie in Wulin saw it and sighed: The eye of gods and men is fortunate indeed not to have fallen. He quickly drafted a notice calling for its circulation. Mao Zijin asked to take sole charge of the woodblocks, to give vent to his fond devotion. When Zijin died, his three sons Bao, Biao, and Yu pursued their father's wish and brought the work to completion. Those in Lingbiao who shared in the search and compilation were the licentiate Wan Tai, the student He Yun, and his kinsman Zhao Ding. Those who assisted Huashou in gathering up what was scattered were Rong Fa of Caoxi, Yuechi of Haizhuang, and Huashou's attendants Jinzhong, Jinzhao, and Jinguang. All shared in the labor of the Dharma milk, and by rule their names should be appended. On the long-zhi day in midwinter of the shang-zhang kun-dun year, the white-robed disciple of Haiyin, Qian Qianyi of Yushan, burned incense, bowed his head, and respectfully wrote this preface.

Majestic and imposing, clear and deep, he lays no ambush within and shows no cliff of pride. His spirit covers heaven and earth; his eyes prop up the Milky Way. Drifting down into the gate of present affairs, he never leaves the far shore of Weiyin. Whether layman or monk, a carrying pole never leaves his shoulder. If he is not the Buddha's or patriarch's servant, he is surely a peddler in the field of awakening. Not until he enters the great blazing furnace will anyone know he is a man of iron. Only when Maitreya descends to birth will this case be settled.

blocks.text: Eulogy for the Portrait of Venerable Kang Senghui of the Kingdom of Kangju, Sent to Master Hanshan (with preface)

inline.s: The Three Kingdoms were a gathering of heroes and also a gathering of weapons. Compassion and prajna had no way in. Then the Patriarch of Kangju crossed the river on a single staff, invoked the Tathagata three times, and his two eyes streamed with blood; the relics dropped into the vase, their light blazed through the six directions, and their blessing reached a thousand ages. At that time the ruler and ministers of Wu were all moved in heart and changed in countenance; from the event they sought out the principle, and knew there was a Buddha and no longer doubted. Once the six paramitas had been translated and the gate of breath meditation was opened, those of either color who attained the pure Dharma eye, and those who entered subtle Chan contemplation, were beyond counting. All this had our Patriarch as its forerunner. Master Hanshan Qing, because he spread the Dharma, was exiled to the miasmic seas, and with the samadhi of compassion he wonderfully made withered bones come back to spring. The layman Shenghua, hearing of this and moved to admiration, specially painted the Patriarch's likeness and sent it up to Caoxi, to be a shadow and echo of the Master. Alas! Where the flesh-body Buddha of Caoxi appeared, from Tang through Song those who drank of Caoxi and attained the Way were never lacking in any generation. Of late Caoxi has run dry and Baolin stands desolate; and again it is through Master Hanshan, whose exile became its waves, that the Caoxi spring lives again. Should the Patriarch's divided body open the eye within the skull, sands as many as the Ganges could not tell it. How could one with a thinking mind measure the depth or shallowness of such merit? The man of the Way Daguan does not understand steering against the wind; he only understands pushing the boat downstream. So he wrote this eulogy:

Kang Senghui came to Wu; Master Qing was exiled to the border. The master of the skull, his diamond eye bulging forth. The misery of the miasmic seas, bones pricking, soul startled; the Master received his sentence and only felt the more the sage's clarity. The poison of Caoxi, all who drank of it died; the Master drank it and dissolved every miasma. He picked up relics with his fingertips, and Kang's greed was greed not for himself; what shame can this heart feel? For spreading the Dharma he was condemned; his life hung by a single thread. Through a thousand miles of miasmic peaks his straw sandals trod it all. The road over the thunder peaks is sheer and high, the hurricane still rising; bowl and vase pass on alone, yet the mark of his tongue shines clear. The demons of southern Yue clap their hands in broad daylight. If I have no mind, that is the bodhisattva's shadow and echo. Kang, with a mind, was foolish and deluded in his essay. With a ceremonial cap he went to Yue: who would not doubt him? At Shitou's parting the heart and diaphragm ran cold. Master Ding blew up the fire and painted Kang's likeness. From the reflected image he gained the mind; when mind is gone, nature is dark. The great function is impermanent; the bell is heard with the eyes. Root and dust, host and guest, gathered in and let go until the dream wakes. In the palm he lifts the jeweled stupa, on the summit of Mount Lao.
Composed by the man of the Way Daguan Ke

blocks.text: A Brief Note on Recording the Complete Dream Wanderings Collection

inline.s: On the seventh day of the first month of the ding-you year, the Censor Gong Xiaosheng came to Haizhuang and brought out the letter of the Minister of Rites, Qian Muzhai. His resolve to circulate the Master's surviving manuscripts was utterly sincere. The monk Huashou read it, and within the space of a few characters was so moved that he asked to leave home; that very day he was tonsured, receiving the Dharma name Guzhi and the courtesy name Qudi. I wrote a verse to aid the cause: A single portion of Hanshan's surviving manuscripts could make Master Chen leave home. The season and the conditions met, and needle drew thread without a hairsbreadth of error. The whole company of fellow students before us helped him put on the robe. And just watch: from a single drop of Caoxi water, a lotus blossoms in the inkstone pool. This shows not only that the Master's light of mind embraced the measureless, but also that each Dharma protector's single ray of mind, together with insentient brush and ink, pushed this monk forward before the Huashou hall to perform the great Buddha-work. And since this monk receives that same light of mind, his becoming a guiding teacher for all people is beyond measure as well. How much more beyond measure is the merit of circulating this book. I therefore record it, to win a single snap of the fingers thousands of miles away. Written by the monk Jinshi on the sixth day of the third month.

The daily record of the Dream Wanderings Collection, and the names of those who edited and re-collated it, are all fortunately preserved here. Tongjiong, styled Ji'an, was the Master's chief seat; the monks of Haizhuang today are all his descendants. Liu Qixiang, styled Zhongdang, entered office by the second class of the examinations and served as assistant prefect of Fuzhou; when the Master's funeral shrine returned to Caoxi and when the manuscripts were collected, he had a hand in both. Jinshi speaks again.
The Dream Wanderings Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Two
A Reply to Censor Zheng Kunyan

As for this matter of the great cause: though it is complete in everyone and ready-made in each, lacking not a hairsbreadth, what can one do when, since beginningless kalpas, the seeds of the root of craving, deluded thoughts and emotional calculations, and deep-soaked habits have so obscured the wondrous clarity that we cannot taste the genuine benefit, and have lived all along on the shadows of deluded thinking about body, mind, and world? That is why we drift through birth and death. The Buddhas and patriarchs came into the world and spoke a thousand words and ten thousand phrases, devising every kind of skillful means, speaking Chan and speaking doctrine, only to accord with capacities and suit occasions, as tools for breaking attachment. Fundamentally there is no substantial dharma to give to anyone. What is called cultivation is simply following one's own mind, cleansing away the shadows of deluded thoughts and habitual tendencies. To apply effort there is what is called cultivation. If a single thought of delusion comes to rest, and one sees through to one's own mind, originally perfect, luminous, vast, pure by nature, utterly without a thing, that is called awakening. It is not that apart from this mind there is something else to cultivate or to awaken to. The essence of mind is like a mirror; the shadows of deluded thoughts and clinging are merely the dust and grime on the true mind. Hence it is said: thought and appearance are dust, consciousness and emotion are grime. If deluded thoughts melt away, the original substance reveals itself of itself, like polishing a mirror: once the grime is clean, the brightness appears. It is simply so. But our habitual defilement has been firm through kalpas, and the root of self-love is deep and hard to pull out. In this life we are fortunate to rely on the prajna that is inherently ours, which perfumes us from within as the cause, and on a good spiritual friend who draws us out from without as the condition. Knowing that it is originally ours, we bring forth the mind and turn toward it, determined to be freed from birth and death. To pull out at once the root and stem of birth and death from measureless kalpas, is that a small matter? Unless one is a person of great strength who bears it bare-bodied and goes straight in with a single blade, it is truly difficult beyond difficulty. The ancients said, it is like one man fighting ten thousand; this is no empty saying. Broadly put, in the final age there are many who cultivate but few who taste the genuine benefit, many who labor but few who gain power. Why is this? Because they have not found the place to lay hold directly, and only work on the words of what they have previously heard and understood, measuring with consciousness and emotion, suppressing deluded thoughts and doing their work at the gate of light and shadow. They first store the wondrous words of the ancients in their breasts, take them as substantial dharma, and make them their own views, never realizing that not one point of this is of any use. This is exactly what is meant by understanding in dependence on another, which blocks the gate of one's own awakening. In doing the work nowadays, one must first cut away understanding and interpretation, and work precisely and solely on a single thought, deeply believing that one's own mind is originally perfectly clean, not hanging by a single thread, round and bright, filling the dharma-realm, fundamentally without body, mind, or world, and likewise without deluded thoughts or emotional calculations. This very single thought is itself unborn. All the various states before one are illusory and unreal; they are only shadows appearing within the true mind. Having seen through them thus, then at the very place where deluded thoughts arise and cease, fix your gaze on them; watch where they arise from and where they cease to. Press hard upon them like this, and whatever deluded thought it may be, one press shatters it, and at once it melts like ice and crumbles like tiles. Never follow them along, and never let them continue. This is what Yongjia meant by cutting off the mind of continuation. For the false and floating mind fundamentally has no root or thread; never take it as a real thing and lodge it in your breast. When it arises, scold it; one scolding and it is gone. Never suppress it, for then it will do as it likes, like a gourd on the water. One need only cast body, mind, and world to one side and single-mindedly raise this one thought, like a sword held across the sky: whether it be Buddha or Mara, cut them all off at once, as one cuts tangled silk, and press on with bare strength. This is what is meant by the straightforward mind and right mindfulness of suchness. Right mindfulness is no-mindfulness. To be able to contemplate no-mindfulness may be called turning toward the Buddha's wisdom. At the very beginning of practice, when one first brings forth the mind, one must deeply believe in the gate of mind-only. The Buddha said the three realms are mind-only and the ten thousand dharmas are consciousness-only. So much Buddhadharma merely explains these eight characters, making it clear so that everyone may believe: the whole broad division of sage and ordinary being is only the two roads of delusion and awakening within one's own mind. All good and evil, cause and effect, apart from this mind, cannot be found as even a scrap of a thing. For our wondrous nature is natural and originally does not belong to awakening, so how could it be deluded? When we now speak of delusion, it is only that we do not understand that our own mind is originally without a single thing, that we do not penetrate the fundamental emptiness of body, mind, and world, and are obstructed by them; therefore we call it delusion. We have all along taken the arising-and-ceasing mind of deluded thought as real, and so in the conditions of the six dusts, in all the illusory transformations, we take them as substantial. Now, when we bring forth the mind and turn toward the upward step of returning to the source, we must strip away all our former understanding entirely; not one point of clever knowing or clever method is of use. Simply see through at a glance the body, mind, and world before you: they are entirely floating light and phantom shadows appearing within your own mind, like an image in a mirror, like the moon in water. Contemplate all sounds as wind passing through trees; contemplate all states as clouds floating in the sky. All are things that change and transform and are unreal. Not only is it so coming from outside; your own mind's deluded thoughts and emotional calculations, all seeds of the root of craving, habitual tendencies and afflictions, are all empty, floating, illusory, and unreal. Contemplating deeply like this, whenever a single thought arises, you must determine to investigate where it goes. Never let it pass lightly, and never be deceived by it. Doing the work thus is drawing somewhat closer to the genuine. Apart from this, to drag in wondrous views and clever methods to fill the gap has nothing whatever to do with it. Even to speak of doing the work is itself a last resort. It is like using troops: weapons are inauspicious instruments, used only when there is no alternative. The ancients said that Chan practice and raising the huatou are both last resorts. Although there are many public cases, only the huatou of investigating Buddha-recitation to its full extent is easiest to gain power with amid the toils of the dust. Though it is easy to gain power with, it is no more than a tile used to knock at the door, and in the end must be thrown away. Still, one cannot do without using it once. If you now use this to do the work, you must believe deeply, rely steadily, and bite down firmly, never wavering. You must not be like this today and like that tomorrow, and then fear you will not awaken, and dislike it for not being wondrous. All these calculations are obstacles; you must first see through them so that no doubts arise at the crucial moment. When the work gains power, outer states do not enter, and only afflictions within the mind rise up without cause; or desires flare up, or the mind grows fretful and oppressed, or various obstacles arise, until mind and body are weary and there is nothing to be done. These are the seeds of habitual tendency from measureless kalpas stored in the eighth consciousness, now pressed hard by the work and all coming forth. Here one must be clearest of all. First one must see through them and pass beyond them, never be enveloped by them, never be toyed with by them, never take them as real things. Only rouse your spirit, summon courage and vigor, raise the huatou of your original inquiry, and right where these thoughts arise, press and pursue them without letup. Here in me there was originally no such thing: ask it, where does it come from, and what after all is it? You must determine to see where it goes. Pressing on like this, you will make gods and ghosts weep, their traces vanish and their tracks hide. You must drive them all out and kill them all, leaving not a thread. Applying effort thus, you will naturally see good news. If a single thought can be pressed through, then all deluded thoughts fall away at once, like the shadows of sky-flowers dropping, like the waves of a mirage settling. After passing this once, you gain measureless ease and measureless freedom. This is where the beginner gains power; it is not yet the wondrous. And when ease and freedom come, you must not give rise to a joyful mind. If a joyful mind arises, the demon of joy attaches to your mind, and there is one more obstacle. As for the seeds of habitual tendency and the root of craving in the storehouse consciousness, firm, deep, and hidden, where the huatou cannot be pressed and contemplation cannot reach, where you yourself cannot lay hold, you must bow to the Buddha, recite sutras, and repent, and also secretly hold the mantra-heart, relying on the Buddha's secret seal to dissolve them. For all the secret mantras are the Buddha's vajra mind-seal. When we use them, it is like holding the vajra jeweled pestle, which shatters every thing; things touched by it become as fine dust. The secret keys of the mind-seal of all the Buddhas and patriarchs from of old are no other than this. Therefore it is said: the Tathagatas of the ten directions, holding this mantra-heart, attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. But the Buddha spoke of it openly; the gate of the patriarchs, fearing it would fall into ordinary sentiment, kept it secret and did not speak of it. It is not that they did not use it. This requires a daily fixed lesson; after long practice it becomes familiar, and you gain much power from it. Only you must not seek divine responses.

Among those who cultivate, some awaken first and then cultivate, and some cultivate first and then awaken. But awakening has the difference of understanding and realization. To clarify the mind by relying on the Buddha's and patriarchs' teachings is awakening by understanding; it mostly falls into views, and in all states and conditions it mostly lacks power, for mind and state stand opposed and cannot merge; every path becomes blocked and many obstacles arise. This is called semblance-prajna; it is not true inquiry. As for awakening by realization: one goes to work plainly and honestly from within one's own mind, pressing on until the water is exhausted and the mountains end, when suddenly a single thought comes to rest and one thoroughly understands one's own mind, like seeing one's own father at the crossroads; there is no further doubt. It is like a person drinking water, knowing for himself whether it is cold or warm, and he cannot disclose it to another. This is true inquiry and true awakening. Then, with the place of awakening, one merges mind and states, cleansing away present karma and the flowing consciousness, deluded thoughts and emotional calculations, all smelted into one flavor of true mind. This is awakening by realization. This awakening by realization also differs in depth. If one works from the root, breaks open the nest of the eighth consciousness, turns over at once the cave of ignorance, and transcends directly in one leap with no remaining dharma, this is the highest of sharp faculties, and what is realized is deep. Others cultivate gradually, and what they realize is shallow. The thing most to be feared is being satisfied with a little. Above all, do not fall into the gate of light and shadow. Why? Because the root of the eighth consciousness is not yet broken, and even if there is activity, it is all on the side of the conscious spirit. To take this as real is much like taking a thief for your son. The ancients said: The student of the Way who does not know the true takes the conscious spirit as it was before; the root of birth and death through measureless kalpas, the fool takes for the original person. This one barrier must above all be passed through. What is called sudden awakening and gradual cultivation means that one has first awakened completely, but habitual tendencies remain and cannot be cleansed at once; so in all states and conditions one uses the principle one has awakened to, arousing the power of contemplation, testing the mind through states. Merge one part of states and you realize one part of the dharma-body; dissolve one part of deluded thought and you reveal one part of original wisdom. This again depends entirely on close and continuous effort, done upon the states themselves, which is more effective.

When people of sharp faculties, faith, and courage cultivate and are willing to do the work, obstacles of circumstance are easy to remove, but the obstacle of principle is hard to dismiss. Of the ailments here I will roughly name one or two.

First, do not crave the wondrous. This matter is originally plain and even, solid and sure, one flavor of the ordinary, with nothing wondrous about it. Hence the ancients said: Awakened, one is still the same as before awakening; one is still the person of old, only not at the old place of walking. There is nothing wondrous. When the work matures, it is naturally plain and solid. It is because our habitual tendencies of understanding are not yet cleansed that prajna perfumes us within, and prajna, perfumed by habit, gives rise to illusions and produces many clever views that cling to the mind; one supposes them to be wondrous and, entering deep, will not let them go. This is precisely the conscious spirit's reflected brightness, the root of deluded discrimination, also called the thorn of views. It differs from the earlier coarse and floating deluded thoughts; it is subtle, a flowing stream of arising and ceasing, also called the obstacle of wisdom. It is exactly what obstructs right views. If a person takes it as real, all kinds of wild views arise. It is most to be guarded against.

Next, do not use the mind to wait for awakening. Our wondrous perfect true mind is originally absolute; it was only because deluded thoughts congealed that mind and state, sense-faculties and dust, stood opposed, and so confusion arose and karma was made. Now the cultivator need only let go of body, mind, and world in a single thought and simply raise this one thought and go forward. Never mind whether you awaken or not; just go on doing it thought by thought and step by step. When the work reaches its place, you will naturally see your original face. Why need you plan ahead? If you use the mind to wait for awakening, then this very waiting mind is the root and stem of birth and death; wait till the end of kalpas and you still will not awaken, because you do not understand the absolute true mind and suppose there is something else. If the waiting mind is not removed, weariness easily arises and one mostly backslides, like giving up because one cannot find what one is looking for.

Next, do not seek a wondrous fruit. The deluded mind of birth and death in sentient beings is originally the Tathagata's fruit-body. Now, in delusion, we turn the Buddhas' wondrous function of spiritual power into deluded thoughts and emotional calculations, discriminating views; we turn the true pure dharma-body into the substance of birth-and-death karma; we turn the pure wondrous land into the states of the six dusts. If in doing the work now a single thought suddenly awakens to one's own mind, then it is like the great smelting furnace that molds the ten thousand forms; this very body, mind, and world are originally the Tathagata's fruit-body; these very deluded thoughts and emotional calculations are originally the wondrous function of spiritual power. The name changes, not the substance. Yongjia said: The real nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory empty body is the dharma-body. If one can awaken to this gate, then the feelings of grasping and rejecting are forgotten, the mind of liking and disliking comes to rest, and every step is the Pure Land of Huazang, every thought the descent of Maitreya. But if one settles the mind on seeking the wondrous fruit first, then this very seeking mind is the root of birth and death; it obstructs right views, and the more you seek the farther away it is. When the strength of seeking is exhausted, weariness arises.

Next, do not give rise to doubts of your own. In doing the work one has all along let go of body and mind, shut off seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, and left the old tracks behind; looking ahead, all is dim, with no place to settle body and life. Advancing, there is no new realization; retreating, one has lost the former abode. If one calculates back and forth, doubt arises, measureless calculations spring up, and one weighs gain and loss; or one forms private opinions and rashly gives rise to wrong thinking, obstructing right views. This must be seen through, and then one enters straight ahead with decision and no further hedging. Broadly, when the work reaches the point where it cannot be done, that is exactly where it gains power; rouse your spirits the more and you will not retreat. Otherwise you fall to the demon of sorrow. Next, do not give rise to a mind of terror. When the work's mindfulness grows urgent and presses the deluded thoughts until a single thought suddenly rests, body and mind may suddenly fall away into emptiness, and one sees the great earth as without an inch of soil, profound beyond limit; then great terror arises. If one does not see through this, one dares not go forward. Or one may take this empty vastness as the supreme wonder. If you acknowledge this emptiness, great wrong views arise, denying cause and effect. Of all these, this is the most perilous.

Next, you must decisively believe that your own mind is Buddha. But Buddha is no other Buddha; mind-only is itself he. For the Buddha's true dharma-body is like empty space. If you penetrate that delusion is fundamentally empty, then the inherent dharma-body appears of itself, luminous and silently illuminating, perfect and all-pervading, lacking nothing and with nothing to spare. Do not let the mind race outward in search. If you abandon this mind and seek elsewhere, the mind will conjure up all kinds of measureless dream states; this is precisely the conscious spirit's transformations, and you must never take them as something extraordinary. Our pure mind is originally without a single thing, without even a single thought; whenever thought arises and moves, it departs from the dharma-substance. People doing the work today never understand that their own mind's deluded thoughts are fundamentally false, and mistake these deluded thoughts for reality; they only set themselves to oppose them, like a child playing with the shadows of a lamp. The more he plays, the less it has to do with anything; and after long toying he frightens himself. There is another kind who fear deluded thoughts and wish they could seize them in one grasp and fling them aside. This is like catching the wind and clutching shadows; the whole day they wrestle with them, use up all their strength, and never have a moment when a single thought rests. Tangled day after day, their faith grows daily wearier, and they say Chan practice has no efficacy, and so give rise to a mind of slander, or a mind of terror, or a mind of backsliding. These are the common ailments of beginners. There is no other cause: it is simply that they do not understand the permanent true mind, the nature that is unborn and undying, and only take deluded thoughts as a real substantial dharma. Here you must certainly pass through. If you would pass this barrier, there is naturally an upward road: you need only inquire apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness, and seek apart from the states of deluded thought. Whenever a single thought arises, whether good or evil, cast it aside at once, never set yourself against it. Deeply believe that within your own mind there is fundamentally no such thing, and simply raise the huatou of your original inquiry with all your strength, like a vajra sword that cuts down both Buddha and Mara. Here you most need great courage, great vigor, and great patience; never calculate back and forth, never be timid. If only you gain the straightforward mind and right mindfulness and step forward boldly, you will naturally be towering and majestic, not entwined by these deluded thoughts, like a hawk slipped from the falconer's sleeve. Through the six periods of the day, amid all states and conditions, you will naturally not be snagged, and naturally gain great ease and great freedom. This is the place where the beginner's first step of work gains power.

The several points above are much like drawing legs on a snake. They are words of expedient means for a time; they are not ultimate and not a substantial dharma. For at the edge of the road, one step out the door, one fears falling into diverging bypaths, wasting effort, and losing time in vain. One must have a truly single gate and transcend the wondrous adorned path; then, as it is said, the steps are even and straight and swift as the wind, and one's progress may be a kalpa doubled in a day. In short, the Buddha's and patriarchs' upward road does not touch upon stages of travel; yet as expedient means for beginners, one must still pass through from here to attain it.
Instructions for the Chan monk Wusheng Lu (spoken at the enclosure in the summer of the yi-wei year)

When the ancients first brought forth the mind, it was truly for the great matter of birth and death, and they resolved on deliverance. Therefore they cut off love, took leave of kin, sought teachers and visited friends, and endured every hardship; thought after thought, their only concern was that the matter under their own feet was not yet clear, and they grieved and ached as though they had lost father and mother. When they met a teacher, it was like an infant finding its mother; if they obtained a word or half a phrase to open and guide their mind-ground, it was like a sick man finding medicine. If a single thought matched, and they understood within, it was like a poor man finding treasure. They staked body and risked life, sank into lowly service, and never shrank from toil, like the Second Patriarch who set his mind at rest by cutting off his arm, the Sixth Patriarch who carried a stone at his waist, Baizhang who bore the labor, and Yangqi who served the assembly. Of all whose names are recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp and whose light shines through the ages, there is not one who did not come through bitter effort. Even the Buddhas of the past, seeking unsurpassed bodhi, gave up bodies and lives as numerous as motes of dust; there was no kind of body they did not take and no body with which they did not practice austerities. Through a hundred kalpas they cultivated the cause, and so drew measureless offerings from gods and humans; even the descendants of the final age still enjoy without exhausting one share of the merit in the white-hair light. How could there be a Maitreya born of himself, a Shakyamuni who came naturally? Bitterly mindful that in the final age we are far from the sages and that the model of the Dharma gate has been swept to the ground: we who have left home do not even know what we are about. From birth we know only to fear hunger and cold and to seek food and warmth. Once we enter the empty gate, we drift with vulgar habits, gossip all day, fill our bellies and indulge our feelings, giving free rein to the six senses and committing every evil. We eat fine food without farming and wear fine clothes without spinning; we waste the gifts of the faithful and squander our time, never knowing where birth comes from or where death goes. How much less do we know that cause and effect are hard to escape, that offense and blessing are never mistaken. When the great limit comes, we are like a stone thrown into water; the fierce suffering of the three evil paths, one recompense lasting five thousand kalpas, and when we may again raise our heads, who knows on what day. To speak of this is bitter and saddening. Looking at the people of the age, the torrent is all like this. Those who cultivate are like picking gold from sand: not that there are none at all, but they are few indeed. Alas! The three realms are a prison, the four kinds of birth a yoke; burned by the great fire, a perilous house of birth and death. How can one moisten the fierce flames, leave all suffering, and reach the place without fear? Unless one is a man of true mettle, endowed with a spiritual root and harboring former seed, one cannot rouse bold courage and transcend straight through in a single leap. You are fortunate to be born where the Buddhadharma is found, to wear the robe as your form, to have met a clear teacher early, and to have the six senses complete. If you do not bitterly bear in mind impermanence, deeply ponder the great matter, reflect on the suffering of hell, bring forth the bodhi mind, mend the past and cultivate the future, and strive day and night, seeking early deliverance, but instead let the days pass idly and indulge body and mind, then when the great limit comes, what use will regret be? Alas, go now, and do not forget these parting words I have urged upon you, so as to betray my own hopes in you.
Instructions for the attendant Qi, given on the boat while I was on my way to Leiyang

The Buddhas and patriarchs teach people to realize at once, within birth and death, the patient acceptance of the unborn. And they are always astonished that within the unborn we falsely see arising and ceasing. Such words are like telling a dream to a market dweller: those who hear are not without wide-open eyes, but they simply have not realized the truth. The point is that what is spoken is not what is heard, and what is heard is not what is seen. The ancients valued actual realization because they wished simply to see through clearly, within the dharma of birth and death, that there is nothing extraordinary there. I once saw a child afraid of ghosts who, walking at night, seemed to see a thing following him and was terrified, and though his loving mother kindly explained that there was nothing there, he would not believe it; only when he came to believe it himself without doubt did it stop. Once he reached the ground of no doubt, even if a ghost were conjured up to frighten him, he would laugh and be released. Long ago, traveling on the frontier, I rode at night with a strong fellow; by the roadside was a stone, and his horse suddenly saw it and shied, nearly throwing him. He then reined in, whipped the horse on, and made it circle the stone dozens of times, and led it to look at it long and hard, and only then let it gallop off. From that time the horse was startled by nothing. From this I know that one who walks the perilous road of birth and death must test the mind through states and only then be done, just so. That is why the Avatamsaka uses Sudhana as its witness: he traveled through a hundred cities and called on many teachers, and even at the mountain of knives and the blaze of fire he still lingered and had to be urged before entering; but when he entered, he indeed gained the great gate of cool liberation. Is this not the meaning of whipping the horse around the stone and making it look long and hard? From this we see that the Buddhas and patriarchs have no other strength at all; they are simply able to look long and steadily at the marks of the world. What people fear is it not birth and death, calamity and misfortune? Yet the Buddhas and patriarchs want people to realize within them the acceptance of the unborn, and they further declare plainly that within the unborn we falsely see arising and ceasing. Ah, what does this mean? Unless one has looked long and hard until one arrives at the ground of no doubt, I think that even the Compassionate Honored One's kind explanations would hardly spare one from terror. Of late, because I spread the Dharma, I met with calamity and provoked the sage's anger, like thunder in broad daylight at which all who hear stop their ears. From my arrest to my release was more than two hundred days, and I passed through hardships beyond describing. From beginning to end, when I looked at the single thought of joy in my mind, it had not diminished at all from former days, and all who observed it were astonished as at something extraordinary. Yet birth and death, calamity and misfortune: others were frightened on my behalf; and when they saw that my joyful mind had not diminished, they were astonished again. I was not frightened by what they feared, and they were frightened by what I did not fear; perhaps there is a Way in this. The attendant Qi traveled more than three thousand li to share my hardship and questioned me in the dark prison; afterwards, by the grace of the sage's favor, I was banished to Lingnan, and Qi accompanied me on the boat. So I write this as a farewell. Alas! On the perilous road of birth and death, that is where fear belongs; let him not hear my joyful mind as a matter of dreams. Another day, when I test you in the field of stillness and extinction, do not take today's words as dream talk.
Instructions for the Chan monk Wuyin Gui

Minggui was a son of the Li family of Western Shu. At seventeen he left home and studied under Chan Master Faguang of Funiu, then bowed at Qingliang and was moved by Manjushri's light, burning off one finger as an offering. He went to the capital to visit Chan Master Bianrong, attended lectures under the master of the seat Gumei, and sought instruction on karmic conditions from the great master Dafang. He visited me at the Haiyin practice place by the Eastern Sea and received the vajra jeweled precepts. I observed that his bone and spirit were lone and hard, fit to be a standard for the Dharma gate, but that thick habits of fame and words kept him from penetrating the true nature. When he first heard my words, they seemed to him as remote as the Milky Way. So I gave him the style Wuyin, No Hiding, and for a year I sang obliquely and spoke sideways, using expedient means to tame him. One day, hearing the teaching that all is mind-only, he suddenly believed and rejoiced, and vowed to take refuge. Three winters and summers he followed me through hardship, and another year later, in the tenth month of the bing-shen year, he came to Wuyang and lodged among the earthen ramparts for several months. I was then studying the Lankavatara and meant to have him enter the room, hoping he would enter the foremost meaning. Suddenly his heart had a thought of returning to visit his family. I held that loyalty to the Dharma gate and filial devotion to teacher and parents are one and the same resolve, and so I instructed him, saying: The Buddha-nature in its entanglement is like divine light within the eye: though light and dark come and go, the illumination stands alone. As the film of obstruction is thick or thin, so the function of wisdom is shallow or deep. Therefore the Buddhas and patriarchs from of old invariably passed through many kalpas, served many teachers, and entered many Dharma gates before they could see the true nature. Why is this so? It is like a person bound fast who cannot untie himself and must rely on another's hands; yet when he is suddenly released and freely moves at ease in the place of use, that is not something the one who untied him can give. Even one of the highest faculties and sharpest wisdom who can awaken to his own mind in a single thought, not obtaining it from another, has surely come from accumulated hardship. It is like returning home from ten thousand li: the single step through the door brings joy for a lifetime, and looking back at the toil and the passes and perils of the journey, they seem dimly like a dream. Moreover, Mahabhidhajnanabhibhu waited ten kalpas and still it did not appear; Shariputra brought forth the mind and turned back midway. Even for sages it is so, how much more for others. Thus we know that to have faith in this great cause, to hold a long-enduring resolve and a determination that goes to the very end, has been rare from ancient times. Looking through the former cultivators, they staked body and life, drew near to teachers and chose friends, often for twenty or thirty years, even to the end of their lives, never changing heart or mind through poverty or success, held by the utmost power of vow, unaltered through kalpas, a thousand years as one day. That is why their light was vast, and once released they became teachers of gods and men. It was not by chance. You, Chan monk, by the power of the prajna you have heard and perfumed in former habits, have not forgotten what came before. Now you are fortunate to be a son of the Buddha and to serve the Dharma gate with such diligence. If you can hold the vajra mind, to the end of this life and even throughout lands as many as the Ganges, with utmost ultimate bodhi and no retreat from the first resolve, then you will spread the Dharma-cloud in the burning house and perfect the seed of wisdom in the garden of enlightenment; and surely this day will be your causal ground. Go now, return to Mount Emei, and see Samantabhadra face to face. If he asks about the transformed people, report that in the miasmic seas and the burning south, the silver world is not diminished. All is well, all is well.
Urging My Young Master Dayi to Return to the Mountain Home to Care for His Parents

When I was young and read history, I admired in secret the conduct of Cheng Ying and Gongsun Chujiu, and thought: Whoever holds this mind in serving as a subject or a son may be said not to have shamed his birth. When I grew up and left home, I said: My Buddha is the Dharma King of the three realms and the compassionate father of the four kinds of birth. If one can hold the mind of those two men in being a disciple, one may be said not to have betrayed one's own spirit. When I read the karmic conditions of the patriarchs in the Transmission of the Lamp, and saw Shenguang cutting off his arm, Chuanzi overturning his boat, Baizhang's relation to Mazu, and Yangqi's to Ciming, I sighed: If one forgets the body for the Dharma as those elders set their minds, why fear that the ancestral Way will not flourish and the Dharma gate will not rise? Alas! A man of mettle in the world, since he cannot exhaust his strength in serving a ruler to win fame and honor his parents, should become a loyal subject of the Dharma King and a filial son of the compassionate father. The ground changes but it is the same; why then stoop to serve petty ends? Therefore I myself have known, since I first had the upward matter, that this mind flutters with thoughts beyond the world; even when confined in a cage or walking the marketplace, I have never failed to place myself amid ice and snow, among a thousand cliffs and ten thousand ravines. In the early Longqing years I lived at the lecture hall of Longhe, and there I came to know Master Miaofeng. Among the crowd I saw his worn countenance and firm bones and knew he was a vessel of Dharma; though we had not spoken, I consented in my heart. In the gui-hai year of Wanli I traveled north to the capital and met him by chance in the market of Chang'an. We sat together beneath the dragon-flower tree, and in one conversation settled the matter of birth and death; so we became companions in practice and wandered together beyond the world. Passing through Hezhong, the patron of Shanyin invited us to his retreat for some months. At that time Zong was still a boy, a novice. The next year I went with Master Miao into Qingliang, placing ourselves amid ten thousand years of ice and snow, where the cold pierced to the bone and we nearly died several times. Then I was fortunate to have a ground of self-confidence. In the ding-chou year the Shanyin patron wrote to Qingliang, entrusting Zong to serve the Dharma gate, and so he was set to work in the stables. Zong cheerfully carried rice and gathered firewood, waded water and trod snow, putting every task first and leaving no gap day or night; the assembly all praised his diligence. Yet he showed no particular talent. In the winter of the xin-si year, in obedience to the compassionate decree, I sought an heir to the throne and made offerings for the late emperor, and held a great assembly at Mount Tai, where ten thousand fingers gathered daily. Zong alone took charge of the tea and soup: by day he moved among them without neglecting a single person, and by night he used his remaining strength for recitation. Then for the first time I knew in my heart that his strength could bear burdens, though I had not yet tested his root of faith. The next spring, the ren-wu year, when the Mount Tai assembly ended, I took leave of Master Miao. He said: I cannot follow you carrying my staff; what will you do, shadowed only by your own form on the long road? Then he looked at Zong and said this boy could take over the duties. So he charged Zong, saying: The ancients followed a teacher for the Dharma and pledged death as their term. You must exhaust your form and strength; if your resolve flags midway, I will not see your face in this life. Remember it. At dawn he set off east and west at once. I stayed with the old man of Longhua to nurse my illness at Zhangshi Rock in the Taihang mountains, and Zong followed alone, diligent in every task. When food was served he would stand in attendance and only eat after we had finished; he read our faces for approval or disapproval and made that his sorrow or joy. When I ate, he ate; if I happened not to want food, he would weep with tears streaming down his cheeks and go the whole day without eating either. I often watched him in private, and for a long time he was the same as on the first day. So I said to the old man of Longhua: This boy is by nature a person of pure filial devotion. When Zixia asked about filial piety, Confucius said that the hard thing is the countenance; this must be what he meant. The next year, the gui-wei year, I went east over the sea and withdrew to cultivate in the depths of Mount Lao, a place human footprints cannot reach, a country of gods and ghosts. I entered the Nalao cave and dwelt there, pushing through brambles, lying in the thick grass, braving wind and waves, passing through perils; the hardships are beyond recounting. Others could not have borne the hardship, but Zong was glad of it in his heart. I too thought I would grow old and die in the hills and valleys and have nothing more to do with the world. After three years, in the bing-xu year, I received the decree of the sage Son of Heaven to distribute the great Tripitaka on behalf of the compassionate and holy Empress Mother throughout the famous mountains of the empire, and to the two Laos as well. Then I sighed deeply and said: Karmic conditions obstruct the Way, and the sages of old grieved over this; blessing is the forerunner of calamity, and former cultivators clearly warned of it. I wanted to avoid it. Zong and his companions, the two attendants An and Gui, came forward and said: Even if the Master has no thought for the world, should he not look up and think of the sage's heart, and of how this exalts the Dharma gate for the welfare of the people? Then I turned my thought and said: It is by the compassion of our sage Son of Heaven, the benevolent and filial Empress Mother, that the Dharma is made a blessing for the altars of state and the common people. How would I dare not exhaust myself and spare no toil to spread the Dharma's transformation and repay the sage's grace above? A loyal subject of the Dharma King and a filial son of the compassionate father: this is truly what I intend. Yet this far corner of the sea is by custom called a land of the uncivilized. Unless we make a vow with one mind, how can we turn the realm of Mara into a Buddha-land? Consider your own hearts: if you can truly take the Dharma as your mind and serve it to the end of your lives, then remain; if not, then go, and do not let another day make of this a worldly dissemination that darkens the eye of gods and men. An and the others assented and came forward, saying: Who is the Master, and what is this matter? May the Master set his mind at ease, take the Way upon himself, and forget feeling for the sake of the Dharma. Would we dare not follow the Master's steps? Thereupon I reverently received the compassionate decree and set my mind on building. In managing affairs, great or small, I entrusted all to Zong, with An and Gui as administrators, and I myself only oversaw the essentials. Relying on the sage's compassionate favor, within three years the monastery was complete and the Way of Dharma flourished; monks from the four directions came daily in greater numbers, until the Eastern Sea had the air of a vast Buddha-land. Gods and men met in secret, and the turning of the transformation was swift and wondrous. The offerings of the mountain gate for the assembly and all the Dharma implements were complete, every hair of them coming from Zong's heart. The scale of what was built was in no way less than in former times, and observers thought it had dropped from heaven or welled up from earth, to be a Dharma banner of the eastern border and a field of blessing for a prosperous age forever. But it had stood only a short while when wild demons vied to rise. In the ji-chou year it met with harassment. Whatever I passed through, not to speak of insults: in bitter cold and sweltering heat I ran along dusty roads, risking the brink of life and death beyond counting. Yet this single thought of lone light in my mind was never for a moment changed, and the resolve of Zong and the others grew only firmer, three years as one day. Someone said to me: The ancients spoke of the family mountain wherever one is; with the Master's lofty attainment and Dharma eye, this place is no more than light dust and gathered froth. Why cling to it so? I said: I have heard that the noble men of the world, dying for their country, die for their country; dying for the Dharma, die for the Dharma. Now by compassionate grace the Dharma has been entrusted to me, and it moreover makes manifest the sage's filial piety. The matters differ, but the charge is the same. To flee danger is unrighteous; to cast away one's commission is disloyal. Unrighteous and disloyal, how could one be a vessel of Dharma? Suppose one held even an inch of territory: if one fled at the approach of danger, how could one face oneself? Better to die at one's post than not to go; better than to live cravenly and lose the scripture. The man assented. Shortly after, the demon wind suddenly ceased. Four years later, in the spring second month of the yi-wei year, trouble rose from within, using demonic affairs as its material, and it moved the sage Son of Heaven to fury. A decree went down to the imperial guards, and many were arrested. At that time An had already gone ahead, and Zong and Gui together met the calamity, while I bore it with my single death. By the grace of the sage's favor I was banished to Leiyang. So in the tenth month of that winter I left Chang'an and parted from Zong. I looked on past events as a dream wandering, and never spoke a single word of worldly feeling. Zong escorted me to the bridge over the river, and I said to him: A man of mettle in the world does not cling in the manner of women and children, much less we who have left home and learned to pass beyond feeling and dharma. But you have followed this old man nearly twenty years, and I have never burdened you with a single phrase of Buddhadharma. I do not know where you have seen this old man. Zong bowed his head and said: Since I began serving the Master, I have known myself to be dull. I dare not seek outside. Above, I do not see any Buddhas or patriarchs; below, I do not see any Chan Way. I only know to do my work and serve living beings. In movement and stillness, leisure and busyness, sickness and calamity, death and life, there is only this one thought, directly observing the Master's mind. Therefore when the Master lives, I live; when the Master dies, I die. I said: My mind has no marks; how do you observe it? Zong said: If the Master's mind had marks, your disciple would not be here today. I laughed aloud and took my leave, going south with only the attendant Shan. In the third month of the next spring we reached Leiyang. Famine had run for years and pestilence raged. I sat in the charnel ground as poisonous vapors steamed and pressed in from every side, and several times I nearly died. In the eighth month of autumn I received orders to come to Wuyang. Those who had once been my disciples came one after another, and when I saw them I cursed them, saying: Each of you has feet to walk the road out of birth and death; who among you lacks a foot of ground? What do you come to see me for? I drove them all off with sharp words. Shortly after, Zong too sought me from Puzhong across ten thousand li, and himself tended the cooking, as tireless as before. The provincial capital of Yue also suffered pestilence, and bones lay over the fields. I ordered Zong to lead men to gather and bury them himself; there were no fewer than ten thousand. I held a ceremony of ferry and rescue to deliver them. When it ended, I urged Zong to return, saying: Why do you cling here? All my life my resolve has been to forget life, for I have learned to pass beyond feeling and dharma. Now, though I carry a spear in the ranks, is not everything Buddha-work? Ten thousand li are next door, the great void an inch away. Seen with the sea-wisdom of the dharma-realm, there is no trace of coming or going, of birth or death; why then sigh and make dream inversions? I only hope you know your mind and reach the root, and with the vajra flame burn through the dust of feeling from kalpas past, so that the root of craving, habitual tendencies, and clinging shadows are all swept clean, with not the least self-deception. Thus you may be said not to betray the Buddha's grace or to fail your own inherent nature; and in this the old man will not have failed you. Otherwise, embracing the Buddha while you sleep, you will still not escape being a companion of Mara, and if you further guard this illusory body, you only add the film of sky-flowers. What in the end is the use? And your parents and teachers are now all old. If you abandon them for this, you are a fool within the Dharma. How is that right faith? Go then, and be good enough to give my regards to all our old friends. Living, we shall meet again; dying, we part forever. Another day, in the eternal stillness and light, looking back on today, it will seem a matter of dreams. Remember it, and do not forget what I have charged you with. (Written on the twenty-fifth day of the second month of the ding-you year, at the travelers' lodging by the earthen ramparts.)
Instructions for the Chan monk Dongwen Cheng

Dongwen Facheng bore a sharp faculty from former lives. He had only just left worldly ties when he met the crane of the water-jiao and quickly saw his error, so he abandoned him and entered Mount Tianmu, where he built a hut with the chief seat Xingrong and his fellows and lived there, polishing the matter under his own feet and enduring firmly for several years. He then studied under Chan Master Daguan and stayed close to him for some time, but since his thought of wearying of clamor and seeking stillness was not yet forgotten, he took his leave and withdrew to Luoxi. Now he has come specially to visit this old man in the land of miasma and ask about the mind-ground Dharma gate. In accord with the Brahmajala Sutra, this old man conferred on him the vajra jeweled precepts. Cheng threw his five limbs to the ground like Mount Tai collapsing: such was his diligence for the Dharma. The old man, having long drunk the miasmic vapors, was out of harmony in the four elements, and so shut the door and withdrew from company, cultivating stillness to rest. Cheng also bowed and returned to the mountain, asking to be given the precepts. So the old man instructed him, saying: The Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of every generation, and all sentient beings with scales, shells, feathers, and fur, down to those in the hells and the three evil paths, and even to those scattered into emptiness and sunk into oblivion: their eyebrows are all tied together, not separated by a hairsbreadth. What they share is the vajra mind-ground; what differs is only feeling, thought, love, and hate. Because the Buddhas and patriarchs make good use of their minds, they turn a filthy land into a Pure Land and transform a mountain of knives into a jeweled grove; even the fiercest suffering and bitterness become the true realm of ultimate bliss. This is no other art: it is simply that within this mind, feeling and thought are not produced and love and hate find no lodging. It is like a clear eye that sees the open sky through and through; how then could inverted phantom flowers of themselves arise and cease? Sentient beings turn away from this, so it is no wonder that all kinds of inversion arise and they bring the fault upon themselves. The Buddhas and patriarchs, pitying such beings, came into the world for one purpose, and they have no leftover dharma to give anyone. They do nothing but point directly at this mind, so that all beings may know their home at once. Hence when the Vairocana Buddha first sat in the bodhi mandala, he too did nothing but proclaim the precepts and dharma of this mind of the Buddhas of the past, the ten directions, and the three times. On the terrace of a thousand flowers, every leaf is Shakyamuni, and he too does nothing but receive and make clear this mind of the Buddhas and proclaim these precepts and dharma. Even the forty-nine years of wagging lips and drumming tongue, of bustling about and bending every way for people, was nothing but causing all beings universally to believe and accept these precepts and dharma. And when at the very end he held up the flower and gods and men stared without understanding, they too were only deluded about this mind-precept. The golden-hued ascetic broke into a smile, and so it passed through twenty-eight transmissions, hand to hand in every generation. When Bodhidharma came from the west and Shenguang stood in the snow, there was no speaking and no words; he too was clearly pointing directly at this mind-precept. It passed through six transmissions, until it reached the old rustic Lu, who, beneath his load of firewood, heard the Diamond Sutra say, One should produce a mind that dwells nowhere, and so suddenly awakened to these precepts: not obtained from another, not given by a teacher, but complete by nature. What was so extraordinary about it? When Huangmei confirmed him, he could say at once, Fundamentally there is not a single thing, so where could dust cling? Therefore the old man of Huangmei could do nothing with him and could only return to his quarters without a word. Even the secret transmission at the third watch was much like exchanging black beans for a person's eyes. How could there be anything extraordinary beyond this? From then on descendants filled the eyes and spread through the world. Those who grasped it died; those who lost it lived. The seventeen hundred men with their drumming tongues and pipings did nothing but illuminate this mind-ground Dharma gate for one another. How could one seek a wondrous awakening apart from this mind? To seek apart from it is to fall into the bypaths of outsiders. Therefore the Brahmajala Sutra says: The mind-ground of Vairocana Buddha, recited in the first arising of the mind, is named the precept of light, the vajra jeweled precept. It is the source of all Buddhas, the source of all bodhisattvas, the seed of Buddha-nature. All sentient beings have Buddha-nature; all consciousness, form, and mind, whether feeling or mind, enter into the precept of Buddha-nature. It also says: When beings receive the Buddha's precepts, they enter the rank of the Buddhas; their rank is already equal to great enlightenment, and they are truly children of the Buddhas. Therefore in the fifty-five stages of progressive practice, those who have not yet seen the Buddha-nature all fall into the paths of stages; only at the very end, in the stage of equal enlightenment, is it said that this person first obtains the vajra mind, the first stage of dry wisdom. Reaching here, one enters directly into the ocean of Buddha-nature. From this we see that, from ordinary being to sage, the essence of becoming a Buddha and a patriarch is no other than this vajra mind; could there be any leftover dharma beyond it? So we know that these precepts are not easy to awaken to; to awaken is to be named the stage of abiding. They are not easy to practice; to practice is to be named the stage of practice. They are not easy to penetrate; to penetrate is to be named the stage of dedication. They are not easy to purify; to purify is to be named the stage of ascent. They are not easy to forget; to forget is to be named the stage of entering the Buddha's rank. Facheng, today you should truly consider: with what mind did you leave home? With what mind did you seek teachers and visit friends? With what mind do you delight in seeking the Buddhadharma? With what mind do you wish to receive these precepts? If you grasp that mind, then the Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of every generation, and all sentient beings together will emit light and shake the earth at the tip of one hair of this old man, and you, through the six periods of the day, will have your eyebrows tied together with all sages and ordinary beings. This is what is called truly upholding the precepts. Otherwise it is perilous; peril means falling. Investigate, investigate, investigate! (Dongwen first took Chan Master Tiezhui Lanfeng as his teacher; the crane of the water-jiao mentioned above refers to Lanfeng.)
Instructions for Lay Buddhists Forming a Buddha-Recitation Society

When our Buddha dwelt in the world and taught the Dharma for the benefit of beings, the four assemblies each gained deliverance; teaching according to capacity, each had its expedient means, and all were made to benefit. It was like timely rain: the three grasses and two trees, without exception, received its moisture, each according to its share, each growing as it should. Therefore the dharmas differ in a thousand ways, but their source is not two. Seen from the Buddha-nature, no being cannot be delivered; seen from one's own mind, no person cannot cultivate. But beings are deluded and do not know it, and there is no true good spiritual friend to guide them, so they willingly fall into sinking and suffer hardship in vain. Therefore when Patriarch Lu first arrived and Huangmei asked where he was from, he answered, I am a man of Lingnan. Huangmei said, Does even a southern barbarian have Buddha-nature? The Patriarch said, People have south and north, but does the Buddha-nature have two? From that one phrase, like thunder startling the hibernating, it spread through the world, but those who know it are few and those who awaken to it are rare. Thus Lingnan is the fountainhead of the Chan Way and Buddhadharma. From the time Patriarch Lu spread the transformation and the Way covered the central plains, yet before his gate the wild grass has lain buried and it has been desolate for several thousand years. Those who discuss it all say it is not a land of good roots; this is not to understand the purport of Buddha-nature. By the grace of the emperor I was banished to Leiyang: I arrived in the spring of the bing-shen year and came to Wuyang in autumn. I finished my commentary on the Lankavatara Sutra among the earthen ramparts. In the summer of the wu-xu year I lectured on it for the disciples who came, and at every session I saw good men come in a steady stream, and I greatly approved of them. Before long more than ten good men bowed and asked to be taught the five precepts for lay Buddhists. I gladly accepted and performed the karma ceremony for them. From then on their hearts turned ever more sincerely and their hearing of the Dharma grew deeper. Pitying that they had not yet awakened and regretting that they did not understand the work of progress and self-deliverance, I gave them the samadhi of Buddha-recitation and taught them to single-mindedly purify their karma, to deeply weary of the conditions of suffering, and to turn toward ultimate bliss. They meet monthly at appointed times, with fixed rules, taking the three periods of recitation of the name, bowing, recitation, and repentance as their practice. I wish to make their faith daily more sincere and their karmic obstacles daily dissolve, and they must make rebirth their vow. If they can truly follow this Way, then though amid the toils of the dust they may be said not to have lived in vain or died for nothing. Is this not true practice? But Buddha means awakened: it is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings. Deluded, one is a sentient being; awakened, one is named a Buddha. The Buddha we recite now is Amitabha of self-nature; the Pure Land we seek is the ultimate bliss of mind-only. If you can keep him in mind without forgetting, then thought after thought Amitabha appears, and step by step you are in your homeland of ultimate bliss. Why then must you look far beyond a hundred thousand kotis of lands for a Pure Land to return to? Therefore it is said: When the mind is pure, the land is pure; when the mind is defiled, the land is defiled. Thus when a single thought of evil arises, the forest of knives and the trees of swords bristle; when a single thought of good arises, jeweled ground and flowered lakes appear. Are heaven and hell, then, anywhere outside this mind? Good men, each of you think it over carefully. You should bitterly bear in mind that the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence is swift; once this human body is lost, ten thousand kalpas cannot restore it. Sun and moon flow like a stream, and time cannot be waited for. If you betray this opportunity and let it pass before your face, when the great limit comes, what use will regret be? Each of you should strive. Take care, take care.
Instructions for the Chan monk Zhenyu

The Chan monk Zhenyu grew up in Luling, abandoned wife and children to leave home, delighted in the practice of detachment, set his aim on famous mountains, and visited good spiritual friends. The phantom man, through phantom karma, was carried astray to the seas of Lingnan, and so the Chan monk was able to come and call on him. Not long ago he took his leave to go to Putuo to pay respects to Master Daguan, who gave him the verse of the Buddha Visvabhu, which he brought back to Wuyang. The phantom man, in the field of illusion, performs illusory Buddha-work, opens the illusory multitude, and teaches the illusory Dharma gate. The Chan monk bowed and asked for instruction, and the phantom man, relying on the samadhi of illusion, taught that all dharmas are states of illusion and dream, and instructed him, saying: Excellent, son of the Buddha; you should consider well. All Buddhas appear through the power of illusion; all bodhisattvas cultivate through the power of illusion; all the two vehicles turn toward stillness through the power of illusion; all outsiders become confused through the power of illusion; all sentient beings are born and die through the power of illusion. As for heavenly palaces and Pure Lands, they are established through the power of illusion; jeweled groves and precious trees flourish through the power of illusion; iron beds and copper pillars are set out through the power of illusion; cauldrons of boiling water and furnaces of coals seethe through the power of illusion; creatures with scales, shells, feathers, and fur fly and dive through the power of illusion; the wriggling and creeping things move and rest through the power of illusion. Even to the utmost of what the Buddhas of the three times have realized and the six generations of patriarchs have transmitted, none of it escapes this net of illusion. How then, Chan monk, can you escape the samadhi of illusion? Try to think carefully: by what cause did you fall into birth and death? By what cause did you enter your mother's womb? By what cause were you submerged in the tangle of love? By what cause did you vow to leave sinking behind? By what cause did you set out to transcend the regions? By what cause did you visit good spiritual friends? By what cause did you tread famous mountains and climb blessed lands, pass through monasteries and enter communities? This year the South Sea, next year Wutai, the year after Emei: you will travel the whole world over, and even through kalpas as dust, exhausting the dust-mote lands of the ten directions and serving the great teachers of the ten directions, none of it will escape the gate of illusion. It is not the ultimate, true place. Yet even so, this is called losing your head and mistaking your shadow; better to go home along the road you came. If you can cut through the knot of illusion in a single step, then the boundless net of illusion splits at once, the shoreless sea of illusion dries at once, the measureless karma of illusion dissolves at once, the boundless practices of illusion are gained at once, and the measureless beings of illusion are delivered at once. This is called using illusion to cultivate illusion, what is meant by the deluded mind of beings being extinguished in dependence on illusion. If not, then even through three lives and sixty kalpas, with Manjushri as your father, Guanyin as your mother, and Samantabhadra as your teacher, if you hope to rely on these close causes to accomplish the matter of escaping birth and death, you will be far, far away. Think it over carefully, and do not say that I am a man of illusion and speak no true words. Investigate, investigate.
Instructions for the Lay Buddhist Yi Zhentan

The roots of goodness of the Buddha-nature are like the seeds of grass in the earth: wherever there is soil, there is none that does not have them. When the timely rain comes, none fails to sprout; but the rain comes early or late, and so the sprouting is quick or slow. Everyone has the seed of the root of goodness. If one meets a great good spiritual friend to guide one, it is like timely rain falling, and one suddenly sprouts, puts forth branches, grows a trunk, flowers, and bears fruit, and there are few who fail to succeed. Hence it is said: When a sentient being comes to plant the seed, the fruit is born again from that ground. There has never been one who reaped fruit without a cause. This is the gate of the Buddhas' and patriarchs' teaching: what matters is observing the faculty and meeting the capacity, guiding skillfully so that one's own nature ripens. There is no other dharma by which to boast and deceive beings. The good man Yi Zhentan was born in a border land and grew up amid toil, so busy with mouth and body that he had no leisure, much less a mind to concern himself with transcending the world and to ponder that the matter of birth and death is great. Had he not planted good roots deeply in former lives, so that they welled up within him and would not be restrained, how could he have responded to conditions as soon as he met them and been able to do so without waiting for teaching? When I was first banished to Leiyang and had not yet crossed the mountains, people said that the border customs loved ghosts and ate flesh and blood, and that there were no good people at all; and they cited the Buddha's words about border lands, the lowly and base, the mleccha kind, counting these as the sixth difficulty, because they cut off the Buddha-seed, destroy good roots, and never hear the names of the Three Jewels. I thought it was so. Then, passing through Dianbai, I saw Tan with several good men bowing their heads to the ground, and I was much astonished. Coming over the Kuteng ridge, they cleared thatch and offered tea to form connections; Tan had initiated this Buddha-work, gathering the faithful to do it. This he did without being guided: is it not that his good roots were fully ripened and the season and conditions had arrived, so that he could not restrain himself, and it appeared on meeting the matter and took shape on meeting the condition? From this we see that the Buddha-nature is not necessarily all good, nor the demon-nature all evil; it follows what one has habituated, and so there is difference. The Buddha's words about evil kinds in the border lands speak of the gravest cases, wishing people to give rise to right faith, be born in the central land, and hear the right Dharma. Seeing Tan's pure sincerity and firm faith, and his establishing of good connections, I saw enough to know that the Buddhadharma is vast and not hard to practice even in the border lands. So I wrote a notice and had Tan and two or three good friends, of one mind and one strength, carry it out; and indeed within a year the work was done, and in three years the transformation spread. Even now, beyond the seas, people on the roads all do Buddha-work, and the turning of the realm of Mara into a Buddha-realm surely began with this one man and this one matter.
