One yin leads to hard ice; one yang brings blazing sun. The mechanism of creation is like this, and so is the mechanism of the Way's transformation. The Buddha said: In a place without Buddhadharma, to establish the Three Jewels is something none but a bodhisattva can accomplish. Bodhisattva in Sanskrit is rendered as a being of great mind. Is Tan not a being of great mind? If from here he advances, with faith that does not retreat and good roots growing deeper, vigorous and diligent, and suddenly awakens to his own mind, then he will cut off birth and death forever and transcend straight through to the other shore of bodhi; and surely this day's single step out the door will be his first ground. Only bring forth a willing mind; you will certainly not be cheated. Strive on.
Instructions for the Chan monk Benjing Gui

The Chan monk Baogui set his mind on protecting the Buddhadharma. He first wrote out the Lotus and other sutras in gold characters, and raised funds to make sandalwood images of Shakyamuni and Amitabha. He lived at Dinghu in Duanzhou and often came to Wuyang to bow and ask for instruction. I instructed him, saying: Our Buddha said that all dharmas arise from conditions and all dharmas cease from conditions. Thus we know that all dharmas arise when conditions meet. Arising when conditions meet, they were not there before they arose; not being there before they arose, though they exist, their nature is always empty of itself. Since the nature is empty, all dharmas fundamentally have no self-nature. Hence it is said: Know that dharmas are always without nature; the Buddha-seed arises from conditions. One who can penetrate that whatever arises from conditions has no nature is a true seed for becoming Buddha. Excellent, son of the Buddha. The sutras you wrote are Dharma; the sandalwood Tathagata you made is Buddha. Your power of faith is the cause, and the transformations you rely on are the conditions. Thus the Buddha arises from conditions and the Dharma too arises from conditions. Within the dharma-nature, Dharma is Buddha and Buddha is Dharma. But I wonder whether you have truly understood whether this dharma-nature is empty or not empty. If you say its nature is empty, then here before your eyes are the Buddha's majestic marks and splendid adornments, blazing with light, crimson as a jeweled mountain; and the eighty-one fascicles of the Avatamsaka's spiritual text, the order of its thirty-nine chapters, the spread of its five rounds of cause and effect, the dense array of its forty-two stages, lacking not a single character; the Lotus Sutra's three rounds of prediction, the repentance liturgies' vast names of Buddhas, lacking not a single person: brilliant and filling the eyes, gleaming and wholly manifest. Can you call this emptiness of nature, with nothing there? If you say its nature is not empty: when the conditions gathered, then paper was paper, ink was ink, gold was gold, and incense was incense. Such paper and ink were all worldly dissemination; such gold and incense were all adornment of evil karma. How then could the name of Buddhadharma have come to be? Seek its original nothingness, and the nature is empty of itself. When the conditions now gather, it is precisely out of worldly gold and incense that the Buddha is made, and out of worldly paper and ink that the sutras are made. Yet the marks of the paper and ink are no different from that time, and their substance is not increased from former days; but once the name of Buddhadharma is made manifest, the minds of reverence and disrespect are separated by a chasm. Those who help accomplish it, though they do not change their former steps, are as far from one another as heaven and the abyss in the mechanism of good and evil. From this we see that all dharmas fundamentally have no self-nature and clearly arise from the meeting of conditions. One who can penetrate that this Buddha and this Dharma fundamentally have no self-nature is a true seed for becoming Buddha. As for the various excellent connections you have made, I wonder whether you made them penetrating no-nature or not penetrating no-nature, or whether through making them you afterward attained no-nature. If you made them penetrating no-nature, then Buddhadharma is in yourself and not in things. If you made them without penetrating no-nature, then Buddhadharma is in things and not in yourself. If through making them you afterward penetrated no-nature, then both yourself and things have no nature. Penetrating that you have no nature, there is no one who makes; penetrating that dharmas have no nature, there is no dharma made. Person and dharma both empty, right and wrong together extinguished, then both yourself and things leave no trace. From what then could you discriminate? In this way merit is inconceivable and bodhi is inconceivable too. Son of the Buddha, to know thus is true knowledge; to practice thus is wondrous practice. Otherwise, to perform an inconceivable Buddha-work with a thinking mind is like holding a firefly in your hand to burn Mount Sumeru: it only adds to your own toil, and how could it ever reach the end? Excellent, son of the Buddha. Contemplate well the Dharma of the Dharma King; the Dharma King's Dharma is thus. You should practice thus and uphold thus. This may be called skillfully transcending all existence.
Instructions for the Chan monk Fajin

Fajin said of himself that his nature had many habits of anger, so the old man, using expedient means to tame him, taught him the Dharma gate of patience and further instructed him, saying: The great master Yongjia said, My teacher saw the Buddha Dipankara and for many kalpas was a sage of patience. Thus we know that the single practice of patience is the first wondrous practice for becoming Buddha. Therefore our teacher, the old man Shakyamuni, life after life was slandered and harmed by Devadatta, and even in this life Devadatta did everything to destroy the Dharma, stopping at nothing, and more than once tried to kill him. Yet at the Lotus assembly the Buddha predicted his future Buddhahood and said: My thirty-two marks and eighty excellences, my supreme wondrous merit, were all accomplished through the good spiritual friend Devadatta. Is this not taking the single practice of patience as the essential practice for becoming Buddha? He also said: Formerly, when King Kalandaka cut my body to pieces, at that time I had no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of being, no mark of life. Had I had a mark of self, person, being, or life, the Buddha Dipankara would not have predicted my enlightenment. From this we see that all the suffering of sentient beings in birth and death is accomplished through the self, while unsurpassed bodhi and the adornments of merit and wisdom come through no-self. Because self and things stand opposed, right and wrong arise; when right and wrong arise, love and hate are established; when love and hate are established, joy and anger multiply; one's nature grows turbid and the mind-ground dark; when the mind-ground is dark, all evils grow; when all evils grow, all suffering gathers; when all suffering gathers, birth and death are prolonged. All this is caused by the self. How grievous is the harm the self does. It is like a strong city with firm soldiers: how easy is it to break? Laozi said: The soft overcomes the hard, the weak overcomes the strong. This is the first ground of the practice of patience. Beings rely on their view of self, firm and hard to break, and so cannot bear one contrary word, cannot be at peace with one opposing matter, cannot endure a single hunger or cold, cannot purify a single thought of desire. All this is not knowing the method of patience, but only increasing the attachment of the view of self. Therefore the Buddha taught his disciples to practice harmony, and he also spoke of the patience of suffering and the wisdom of suffering, and of the patience of the unborn, which is only attained at the eighth ground. Thus we know that from the patience of dharmas to the patience of the unborn, wondrous practice is perfected and the Buddha-fruit accomplished. Is the single practice of patience then a shallow thing? Hence it is said: In all that one does, one should be patient. That means: in every place where a thought moves, test it with patience; at every place where a foot lifts, put patience first; in every turn and movement of bearing, hold it with patience; in joy, anger, sorrow, and delight, verify it with patience. Then the mind will not dare move rashly, the body will not dare act rashly, affairs will not dare be done rashly, and feelings will not dare be expressed rashly. Therefore Laozi said: I dare not be first in the world. To dare not is another name for patience. Because one does not dare be first in the world, patience is the first practice for becoming Buddha. In this way patience is great and I am small; therefore patience can cover me and can cover things as well. The virtue of benefiting self and others is found nowhere else. Hence it is said, the robe of gentleness and patience; this is what is meant. The Chan monk asked for a Dharma word, so I entitled it Patience as the Robe. Chan monk, strive to put it into practice, and do not make it mere talk on the lips, nor use it to win a living.

Instructions for the Chan monk Xingchun

As for this matter, it is like the blue sky and the white sun, at the crossroads, on the road to Chang'an: coming and going, who does not meet it face to face? Has it ever hidden a hairsbreadth? Or again, it is like the bright sun adorning the sky: mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, insects, creatures with scales, shells, feathers, and fur, those that fly and those that dive, those that move and those that grow: who does not share equally in its use? Even one blind from birth, though he has never seen it, is never without its benefit. How then should it be lacking or hidden in your case alone, that you must spend money on straw sandals, climb mountains and wade streams, and seek teachers and friends far and far away, searching for it only in deep mountains and lonely valleys, and only then attain it? You simply do not understand, and so you do not cut off the root of life in the single step beneath your own heel; you are toyed with by all the habitual tendencies of idle discourse from measureless kalpas, exactly like one bewitched by a ghost in broad daylight: eyes wide open, mouth open, babbling nonsense at people, never knowing where it comes from or who is driving it. All day and all night you are soaked and tangled, drifting with the waves, wave after wave, kalpa after kalpa, never knowing what you are doing, never knowing what sort of person you originally are. And when you suddenly wake from the dream, you feel great shame, even to wringing your wrists, stamping your feet, grinding your teeth, and beating your breast, wishing you could leap in one bound onto the crown of the Buddhas' and patriarchs' heads. But when you meet a state or encounter a condition, in the blink of an eye you fall unwittingly into the black mountain and the ghost cave. This is the common ailment of all in the world who have the will to study the Way; how could it be so only for Chan monks? Yet the root of the ailment lies simply in not understanding one's own mind, in being toyed with by habitual tendencies. All my life this old man has had the will for this one great matter, and I regret only that my prajna conditions are shallow and my habitual tendencies unusually thick, and that I have no forge and bellows such as the truly clear-eyed teachers of old. From the time I resolved to leave home and began wandering to study the Way, even to entering the mountains amid ice and snow and cold cliffs, to the very place of a thousand deaths and one life, all the various tricks and understandings in me were of no use whatever here. Only when I sat in a cold place, covered by my quilt with my head wrapped up, did I suddenly glimpse a bit of news from before my parents were born, and then, looking back at all the former inversions, they were all matters of a dream. And I hated myself for being dragged along by other karmic conditions and falling into all kinds of illusory states, until I skirted ten thousand deaths and won one life. What saved me was a bit of lone light won amid freezing and hunger, useful everywhere; I made all kinds of adverse and favorable states into the forge and the hammer, to temper my habitual tendencies, those coarse heavy shadows of conditions and dust. Even now I do not know how the pass of birth and death stands; I may not have understood the Chan Way or the Buddhadharma. But as for truly believing that the mind itself is Buddha and not seeking a single point from another, I make that the tool for passing the years. Of what else is there any need to speak? Chan monk, you are about to set out, and to ask this old man for a Dharma word is like seeking Chang'an inside the Hanyuan Hall. If you can understand the one point of the step before your own feet has moved, and can pick it up and put it down, then even in daily seeing forms and hearing sounds, before your eyes open and before your ears take it in, you can already see with the ear and discern with the eye, and will never again bob up and down in the nest of birth and death, in the ranks of habitual tendency. This is what is called not touching the road: one step already transcends, and then the Buddhas and patriarchs have no place to stand, and old man Yama can do nothing with you. Thus you will not betray the grace of Xuelang's guidance, nor betray the one seed of your own that you have carried through a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives, nor let it be steamed rotten by the three poisons of habitual tendency; and you will not betray this old man's speaking up for you today in the field of spears and halberds. If it is not so, then even if you master the three baskets and twelve divisions, what good is it? Like the man of old, though able to dress and eat, what would you call him? As for this old man's words today, they are much like putting boots on a wooden man and a hat on a stone woman. The ancients said: Setting out on foot in early autumn, all of you need only go where there is not an inch of grass for ten thousand li. Tell me, what is the place of not an inch of grass? Investigate, investigate, investigate.
Instructions for the Seat Master Miaozhan

From of old the ancients left home for the great matter of birth and death, and the Buddhas and patriarchs came into the world solely to reveal this matter. There is no other Buddhadharma apart from birth and death, and no other birth and death apart from Buddhadharma. It is as it is said: deluded, birth and death begin; awakened, the round of rebirth ceases. Thus we know that the ancients' inquiry sought the crucial point and the ultimate only on the road of birth and death; they did not, apart from this, take some extraordinary thing as their task among paper, ink, and words, or in the three vehicles and twelve divisions of teaching. That is why Bodhidharma came from the west and set up no dependence on words, only to awaken completely to one's own mind, taking this mind as the root of all the sages and ordinary beings and the ten realms, both dependent and direct retribution. To awaken to this mind fully is the supreme Mahayana; to awaken slightly is the two vehicles; not to awaken is the ordinary person. If one awakens yet does not abide in it, realizes yet gains nothing, that is the upward road that transcends sages and ordinary beings and leaves birth and death behind. Students of recent times are ever farther from the sages and do not see the true conduct of the ancients, which was to pass through one by one the states before them in daily life and the shore of birth and death. In this very daily life, not departing from a single dharma and not abiding in a single dharma, never letting anything pass lightly anywhere, this is genuine effort. In this very moment, every sound and form, every adverse and favorable state of love and hate, wherever you pass through one by one, this is the true gate of awakening. In this very place of awakening, every head and every dharma is the true Buddhadharma. It is not that Buddhadharma exists only when one listens to a seat master strike the bell and beat the drum, mount the flowered seat, open a great mouth, learn the howl of a wild jackal, and, with ears cocked and head bowed, eyes closed, and robe draped, sits there. That is why the youth Sudhana traveled south through a hundred cities and called on good spiritual friends as numerous as dust motes in the Buddha-lands, and so awakened to the gate of liberation of every dust mote and every land. Yet the Dharma gates are beyond counting; how could there be as many good spiritual friends as dust and lands? You must understand that lands and dust motes are simply the deluded thoughts, emotional calculations, and dust of feeling in our daily life. If in daily life, at the place where thought arises and moves, at the place where the root of feeling is knotted firm, at the place where love and hate cross and are hard to untie, at the place where greed, anger, delusion, and pride and all habits are hard to wear away, one applies the awl to the painful place at the root, sees through each one and passes through each one, then this itself is the true teacher; one at once ascends the unhindered, free, and greatly liberated unsurpassed Dharma gate. Apart from this, what other teacher is there to call on, what more extraordinary Dharma gate is there to enter?
Instructions for the Venerable Jing of Lingzhou

Long ago I traveled to Haimen and climbed Miaogao Peak, entering the samadhi of boundlessness and the room of the Lankavatara. There I saw the manuscript of the Lankavatara Sutra written in the hand of old man Su Dongpo on behalf of Zhang Fangping, which he and Chan Master Foyin left as a permanent holding for Jinshan. At that time every pore of my body was filled with delight and gladness, like a hundred grasses sprouting in spring, and I did not know why it was so. Afterwards, when I examined the teachings to confirm it, I understood that it was a habitual tendency bursting forth from within, perfuming me without my being aware. From then on, wandering like cloud and water, this broad, open, empty, luminous, and vast state has always been like a great perfect mirror hanging before my eyes. Lately, toyed with by illusory karma, I went straight to the land of miasma; the boat passed the mouth of Caoxi, went down the Zhenyang gorge, passed Little Jinshan, and reached Yangcheng. I had no leisure to climb and gaze, and only in the autumn of the wu-xu year did I first take in its beauties. With the Venerable Jingxin I passed the Dongpo Hall and read the poem on awakening to a former life, and again I felt a pang of loss, as if seeing an old journey in a dream. Thus I know that heaven and earth are one illusory device, the ten thousand dharmas one illusory thicket, coming and going one illusory trace, death and life one illusory arena, rivers and mountains one illusory realm, creatures with scales, shells, feathers, and fur one illusory thing, sages and ordinary beings one illusory multitude, and you and I one illusory meeting. The Venerable has brought his mind low before the white Dharma and recites the Diamond Sutra daily as his fixed lesson, so that old defilements are suddenly wiped away and the light of mind gradually clears. He is willing to scrape away grime and polish the brightness, and is not to be compared with those who drift idly on the waves of the sea of karma. Lately he brought a scroll asking for a Dharma word as provision for his practice. This old man thought sharply of the former journey to Haimen. Now, in this place, seeing Dongpo as if seeing a former life, I sighed over how human life, birth and death, illusion and transformation, coming and going, are matters of a dream. If one illumines them with the sea-wisdom of the dharma-realm, then the three times and ten directions are equal in this moment; heavenly palaces and Pure Lands lie level along one road; mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are utterly without difference; cauldrons of boiling water and furnaces of coals are in reality cool; grasses, trees, courtyard moss, wind-blown sails, sand birds, the changing shapes of mist and cloud, the rising and setting of sun and moon: all that the eye meets is nothing but the samadhi of universally manifesting the body of form. What we who study the Way value is the vajra right eye that blazes through the darkness of beginningless ignorance and brings forth the original light of wisdom, taken up into the daily life before us: in the moment of coughing, spitting, swinging the arm, raising the brow, blinking the eye, lifting the spoon, raising the chopsticks, suddenly manifesting the stainless dharma-body of self-nature. Such a one is called a person who has attained liberation. Even when Subhuti awakened to prajna, he wept with tears before the Buddha, saying that in truth there is nothing attained that is called an arhat. Among all the dharmas of the world, could any surpass this prajna? Yet prajna is no other thing: it is the light of the mirror of our own mind. Yongjia said: Till now the dusty mirror was never polished; today at last it is clearly wiped and examined. The Venerable is named Jingxin, Mirror Mind. Is it that you take the mind as a mirror, or that you use a mirror to reflect the mind? If you take the mind as a mirror, then old Lu said, The bright mirror is also not a stand; if not a stand, there is no mirror to lodge in. If you use a mirror to reflect the mind, the mind fundamentally has no marks; from what then would you reflect it? Thus it is neither mind nor mirror; neither mirror nor mind. Mind and mirror both denied, from what is the name established? Then the Venerable's name is a false name; and if the name is false, the true is not true either. Then the prajna you read, how could it have any words, phrases, or characters lodged at the tip of your lips and cheeks? If the Venerable can awaken to this Dharma gate, then the light on the river and the color of the water, the speech of birds and the sound of the tide, all proclaim the true mark of prajna; morning bell and evening drum, seeing off and welcoming, are all Subhuti sitting quietly in the stone chamber seeing the dharma-body. Then the Lankavatara written by Dongpo, the cutting of the woodblocks by Foyin, and this old man's bearing today the conditions of three lives and passing this mountain again, with the Venerable happening to take up this scroll to ask for instruction, are not to be called again the dream talk of a former life. The sutra says: All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and like lightning; thus should they be contemplated. If the Venerable does not obscure the original cause, then when his habitual tendencies burst forth he should take this scroll and read it, and before he knows it his deluded thoughts, inversions, and dust of feeling will melt like ice and crumble like tiles.
Instructions for the Student Ou Boyu

I have often said that all sages and ordinary beings alike accomplish their worldly and world-transcending works through the power of their vows. Thus we know that when we set our will on the matter of nature and life, our will is set on leaving birth and death; when we set our will on fame and wealth, our will is set on entering birth and death. Our teacher said: The vast ocean of wisdom is transformed into the ocean of the karma of birth and death; the precious luminous wondrous nature is obscured and becomes the karma-nature of birth and death of greed, anger, and delusion. From this we see that in our own nature the source of the true and the false is already not two. If we know that we enter birth and death through greed, anger, and delusion, then we can also use greed, anger, and delusion to leave birth and death. There is a proverb: He who hates little is no noble man; he who is not ruthless is no true man. I often think of how Goujian, because of the shame of Kuaiji, resolved to avenge himself on Wu, and so for more than twenty years slept on brushwood and tasted gall, wearing no second color of cloth and eating no second flavor of food, until he finally destroyed Wu and became hegemon. We who study the Way look upon birth and death through kalpas, imprisoned and humiliated in the prison of the three realms: is that merely the shame of Kuaiji? Greed, anger, and delusion rob us of the light of our wondrous nature and break down our house of nirvana: is that merely the enmity of Wu? Yet we take it sweet as honey and play and feast with it, without the least shame or resolve of hatred. We may be said to be greatly ignorant of our own root. Can such a one be called a true man? Boyu, if you have the will for this, you should gnash your teeth.
Instructions for the Student Feng Wenru (geng-zi year)

The first thing for one who studies the Way is to bring forth a decisive and long-enduring resolve, even to the end of this life and through three lives, five lives, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand lives, and on through kalpa after kalpa and life after life, resolving with certainty to make awakening its term. If one does not awaken to this mind, one will certainly not stop. Even if one falls into the hells and the three evil paths, or passes through a furnace or a mare's womb, one vows never to abandon this decisive resolve to become Buddha, and never to retreat from today's faith because of suffering. It is like a person who resolves on a journey of ten thousand li, deciding on the place he will reach as his goal: from the day he steps out the door and sets foot on the road, until he enters the gate of that place and sees the person he seeks, until he ascends the hall and enters the room, joins with him in joy and intimacy, and finally forgets himself entirely. Only this can be called a decisive resolve. If one lacks this clear-cut decisive resolve and merely says one wants to set out, yet looks back at all the things one loves and cannot put them down, or drifts and puts it off, the mouth going while the mind does not, or if one is fortunate enough to have relatives and friends of great strength who urge one out the door, and once on the road one wanders aimlessly, or meeting a band of singers or a scene of wealth and rank grows greedy for the immediate pleasures of ear and eye and forgets the thought of not yet having left the door, at a loss where to turn; or midway the conditions turn bad and one runs into evil friends and evil conditions and ends up with an empty purse and exhausted funds, and sickness drags on, and one hesitates and turns back, giving rise to measureless suffering; or the body grows weary and, long soaked in wind and frost, cannot bear the hardship, and one thinks of turning back; or near the gate one meets a single circumstance, state, or matter gone wrong, or hears a false report and takes it for true, so that one is about to see the person and does not, and reaches the gate and cannot enter the room: all such cases waste their toil and never truly arrive at the ultimate place. This is because at the first arising of the mind there was no decisive resolve. If one is like this, one cannot accomplish even a small worldly matter of fame or fortune, much less the unsurpassed Buddha Way, the ending of birth and death, the realization of bodhi. Hence it is said: The Buddha Way is long; one must long endure bitter effort before it can be accomplished. How could one seize quick results and seek speedy success? Yet even so, with a decisive resolve one still needs true insight. If one's insight is not true, one sets one's will on what one should not and does what one should not, and again the effort is wasted. Having this resolve in seeking the Way, one must deeply believe that one's own mind in its very substance is Buddha, originally pure and without a thing, originally luminous and vast. If in daily life one cannot taste this, it is only because the illusory body and the four elements confine and obscure one, and a mere deluded floating mind blocks one, so that it is hard to see through. To pass this hinge of birth and death is not merely some tens of thousands of lives and kalpas away. Since we know this mind and believe it without doubt, the resolve we bring forth today, determined to make awakening its term, is the first step out the door; and receiving today the guidance of a good spiritual friend is what urges us out. As for being urged out onto the road, the various states along the way, the various hardships, the various hesitations, whether one lingers or does not, whether one retreats in idleness or not, all must be weighed by the student on his own ground beneath his own heels; they are not something a good spiritual friend can give. Feng Wenru, since you have the will for this, lift your eyebrows and look at the first step out the door beneath your own heels.
Instructions for the Student Zeng Liufu (ren-yin year)

The sage uses his mind as a mirror: he neither sends nor welcomes; things come without sticking and go without trace, because he is utterly empty and so responds to the ten thousand existences. Hence Laozi said: Without going out the door, one knows the world. How could this be reached by deluded thought, calculation, scheming, cleverness, or conjecture? What is called vast and utterly impartial is the mind of the sage. The clever and scheming men of past and present say of themselves that no thought escapes them and no wisdom can match theirs; so they adorn cleverness and make themselves foolish. It is that the light of their mind has not broken through and their original substance is not clear; they fall into the net of beginningless deluded thought and take it for great wisdom, like holding a firefly to vie with the blazing sun. Zeng, if your will is set on the Way, you should encourage yourself with this.
Instructions for the Attendant Zan

The attendant Zhenzan painted a small portrait of me, burned incense, bowed, and asked for a Dharma word. The old man suddenly seized his staff and chased him, saying: You serve me morning and evening, and still do not know to feel reverence; how then can a portrait in paper and ink be your model? You hear the Dharma teaching with your own ears at every turn, yet it passes like spring wind through the ear; how then can stale words on paper be your standard? Since you resolved to leave home and seek the mark of detachment, and yet do not decisively resolve to practice the detachment of conduct, are you truly leaving home, and truly for the sake of birth and death? Your own mind is deluded and confused; you race outward in search, not knowing that suddenly resting the mad mind is the secret essential for becoming Buddha. You cling pettily to the illusory as real, losing your head and mistaking your shadow, with no term of escape. Even if this old man sat inside your chest, you would take it for a feverish delusion. The Buddha said: If the mad mind does not rest, when it rests, that is bodhi. The supreme pure luminous mind is fundamentally not obtained from outside. If you can be thus, you may be called one who sits in Chan, and need not labor to bow to teachers everywhere, for you will enter measureless Dharma gates yourself. This is called according with the nature of awakening. Why then wrap up this old man? Think for yourself: through the six periods of the day, setting aside dressing and eating, greeting guests and entertaining visitors, turning, bowing, and looking up, coughing, spitting, swinging the arm, and idle talk and jest, what is your own original face? If you see through here, I will allow that you have glimpsed one hair of this old man's eyebrow. If not, you are a thousand li away though face to face.
Instructions for the Chan monk Mingzhe

In the fourth year of my banishment, the summer of the ji-hai year, I lectured on my new commentary on the Lankavatara Sutra at the Traveler's Rest Hut by the Green Gate in Wuyang. The Chan monk came several thousand li to call on me in the land of miasma. Seeing that he was careful and sincere, I put him in charge of the communal food, intending also to let him understand the three virtues and harmonize the six harmonies, gather in the one mind and cultivate the ten thousand practices. The Chan monk obeyed my orders and had labored diligently for more than half a year, when, having drunk the miasmic vapors, he was soaked in them and fell ill. Seeing that his four elements could not hold up and that he could not bear the many duties, he begged to cross the mountains northward and seek a pleasant place to rest and recover, and so took his leave. The old man therefore encouraged him, saying: Do you think suffering and pleasure are different places, and birth and death have a this side and a far side? You do not understand that the four elements are a borrowed thing, suffering and pleasure an illusory arena, birth and death night and morning; nor that the mind is the source of all evil and the body the root of all suffering. Originally one is deluded and the mind becomes consciousness; one clings to the false and takes it as the body, inverting birth and death and rising and sinking in the road of suffering, and one does not know how many thousands of ten thousand kalpas this has gone on. It is like dreaming one is racing along a perilous road, terrified and panicked, seeking escape and unable, wanting to leave and not getting out, sorrowful and miserable, with no door to call for help, spirit and strength exhausted, with no way to rest even for a moment, saying to oneself that one will fall forever into sinking, and so one resigns oneself to drowning. How could one know that by crying out with all one's strength and suddenly leaping up and waking, all the former sorrow and bitterness become a laughing matter? Since one is now awake, how different from the former seeking of escape: as different as heaven and earth. Look at yourself now: your sick and suffering moaning, your thoughts of going or staying and seeking release, are exactly like a matter in a dream. You cannot call out and wake yourself, and I am shouting aloud for you and still you do not know it. So you will be in the long night, with no hour of waking. Why then take the illusory and false as sweet and bitter, and take the dream as your true home? Now that you have met the call and do not wake, who else is there to call you? Alas, alas. For the blind and inverted, in the long night, to wish to see the light of the sun of wisdom with the conditions of a day like this is difficult beyond difficulty. Think it over. If you suddenly wake with a start and turn your head around, the pass of birth-and-death feeling will split open at once; that is the hour of breaking the dream house and leaving the perilous road.
Instructions for the Chan monk Shu Zhong'an on Dwelling in the Mountains

The Chan monk Shuzhong was about to clear thatch on Nanyue and asked for the essentials of mountain dwelling. The old man therefore instructed him, saying: The Way is not in the mountain, yet to dwell in the mountain one must first see the Way. To see the mountain and forget the Way, the mountain becomes an obstacle at the root; to see the Way and forget the mountain, then whatever the eye meets, following conditions, is nothing but the Way. This is the famous saying of the ancients and the true instruction of Yongjia. You now intend to dwell in the mountain: is it that you have seen the Way and will then dwell, or that you will dwell and then see the Way? If you see the Way and then dwell, then dwelling is abiding, and if you abide, the Way is not the true Way. If you wish to dwell in the mountain and then see the Way, the Way fundamentally does not abide; if you abide, the Way is not in the mountain. What then will you take as the Way, and where will you dwell? You merely take the mountain as a mountain, not understanding that in daily life before you, body, mind, and states are all mountains. The teaching says: Birth, old age, sickness, and death are pressed upon us by four mountains. It also speaks of the mountain of the five aggregates, the mountain of self and others, and the mountain of nirvana. Yet nirvana is mind, self and others are states, and the five aggregates of body and mind are the cave of birth, old age, sickness, and death. Nirvana in Sanskrit is rendered as stillness and extinction. The illusory body, mind, and states all belong to movement and disturbance; but as to their root, the true and the false are not two, and movement and stillness are both such. It is only because of the division of delusion and awakening that there is the difference of sage and ordinary being. Deluded, nirvana becomes birth and death; awakened, birth and death realize nirvana. Thus we know that the mountains of the five aggregates and of self and others are originally the peaceful dwelling of nirvana. Then all sages and ordinary beings, going out from birth and entering death, have never failed to dwell in this mountain; and you have long lain and lived in it through the long night. Why then do you now wish to dwell in it? If you take liking and disliking, grasping and rejecting as provision for entering the Way, it is like fleeing drowning and throwing yourself into fire. Hence it is said: I wish to flee it, but cannot flee; beyond the great square all is filled up. It is also said: If the mad mind does not rest, when it rests, that is bodhi. The essential of entering the Way lies only in resting the mad mind, blotting out seeing and hearing, cutting off knowing and understanding, forgetting subject and object, and bringing right and wrong to rest, stilling this mind. It is certainly not in fleeing the body into mountain valleys, eating one's fill and lying about, indulging laziness, and nurturing pride, as the wonder of the Way. Dhuta in Sanskrit is rendered as shaking off, because it can shake off the dust and afflictions of the guest. Merely to purify one's mind: that is the Way of all Buddhas. Strive on.
Instructions for the Chan monk Ji (xin-chou year)

The Buddhas and patriarchs came into the world and showed people only the fundamental Dharma; fundamentally there is no leftover dharma and no substantial dharma. Their only wish was to let everyone know for himself what he originally has. Even what the three baskets and twelve divisions and the patriarchs of every generation point to is nothing but wishing people to recognize at once what they originally have; they fundamentally do not have them seek outward. Because people of the world do not know that their own portion is complete and suppose there is something else, they seek it in all doctrines, investigate it in public cases, hunt for it in paper, ink, and words, and even take all kinds of tricks and calculations as studying the Buddhadharma and as Chan practice for ending birth and death; and they take all kinds of toilsome worldly undertakings as world-transcending practice. Seen today with the right eye, none of it has anything to do with it. Why? Because all of it is made with deluded thought, like a matter in a dream, since the mind and consciousness are not yet left behind. The ancients said: What damages the wealth of Dharma and destroys merit is none other than this mind, intellect, and consciousness. Yet the root and stem of birth and death through measureless kalpas is planted in the nest of discriminating feeling; and one further waters it with the water of craving, fertilizes it with the mud of desire, and smokes it with the fire of ignorance, so that the sprouts of all suffering grow. Even the views of Buddhadharma all fall into the idle discourse of outsiders and only increase the root of suffering; they are not the essential for escaping suffering. Disciples of the final age are far from the sages and do not receive the guidance of clear-eyed, true teachers; they often rely on their own cleverness and give rise to great wrong pride. Not only do they use the views of Buddhadharma to bully people and look down on things, taking this as the secret of surpassing Buddhas and patriarchs; they also take worldly writings, the scriptures of outsiders, and evil views and arguments, and with the sharpness of tongue and the gallop of wit, take these as the means to pry open heaven's gate, thinking that old man Yama certainly cannot control them. Nor do they know any longer that there is worldly and world-transcending cause and effect. This is all because they do not know their own mind and do not know the fundamental Dharma; in the one step beneath their own heels they have nothing to do with it, and they merely rely on their foolish madness and increase the inversions of a dream. Chan monk, since you came forth, you have known how to draw near to teachers and choose friends in this way, to practice austerities in this way, and by all kinds of conditions to seek the Buddha Way. Do you know what you originally have and so bring forth the mind, or do you not know what you originally have, and bring forth the mind and then seek it by the direction of teachers and friends? If you know what you have and then bring forth the mind, then you would not go wandering like this. If you know it only after the instruction of teachers and friends, then you need not do as you do, still walking on the outside in foolish madness. As for your present affair of shutting the gate and copying sutras, what of it? The Flower Ornament is the sutra of entering the dharma-realm. Tell me, what is the dharma-realm, and how does one enter it? If you can raise up a heart and guts of raw iron and open wide the vajra eye, and kick over the cage of birth and death with one foot so that, like a lion slipped from its chains, you roam at ease; then see how Sudhana, when he first brought forth the mind and first met Manjushri, broke through this hinge and knew at once how to swagger south through more than a hundred and ten cities and call on teachers numerous as dust motes. After that even the Vairocana Buddha could do nothing with him, and he became equal to the dharma-realm, equal to empty space, equal to Vairocana, equal to the practices and vows of Samantabhadra. Had he not at the very first met such a person to point out such a matter, I fear he would still be buried in a single dust mote, tightly shut like the great iron enclosing mountain, and not merely in the death gate you face today. How could he accomplish in one life the cause and effect of kalpas and settle the debts of grievance from before? Chan monk, if you do not believe this old man's words, then take up and put down, turn sideways and upright, at the tip of a single hair, and look closely with your own eyes. If you truly see through with one glance, then you will believe that this old man does not deceive you, and believe that the Vairocana Buddha does not deceive you, and the patriarchs of every generation do not deceive you; and trusting in your own mind, you will not deceive yourself either. If not, then listen to the final phrase.
Instructions for the Chan monk Zongyuan on Dwelling in the Mountains

In the fifth year of my exile beyond the seas, the spring of the geng-zi year, the Chan monk Zongyuan Shao came from Nanyue with Fu of Qingtang, accompanied by the two men Wuxin Rong and Foling Qian. The old man shared food and rest with them, and we spent the summer retreat among the earthen ramparts for nearly half its course, then moved again to Donghua. After the retreat ended they each took their leave. Zongyuan bowed and begged a single phrase as the essential for dwelling in the mountains. The old man wiped away his sweat and instructed him, saying: To enter the deep mountains and dwell in a hermitage is the first condition for entering the Way for the Buddhas and patriarchs from of old. Our original teacher, the old man Shakyamuni, cast away the golden wheel, took leave of kin, and cut off love, went into the snowy mountains, and buried himself a thousand feet deep in ten-thousand-fathom cold cliffs, until magpies nested on his head and reeds pierced his knees, and he did not even know the six years of freezing and hunger, flesh and bone barely holding together, in that bitter, empty, lonely state. Then one day he saw the morning star and awakened to the Way, lighting up the long night alone. At once dragons and gods encircled and guarded him, gods and ghosts revered him; he became teacher of gods and men and eye of the world, and to this day his light shines over the four continents and his Way flows through a hundred million lands. Those who hear his name rejoice; those who see his mark take refuge; kings and ministers revere him and those with understanding turn their hearts to him; Brahma temples and jeweled palaces, splendid and adorned, are found far and near, and after a hundred generations he is as if alive. That his blessing flows without end and his merit endures without decay was all won from six years of freezing and hunger in the snowy mountains. Even the descendants of later ages still enjoy the four requisites without exhausting it. This is the one model of mountain dwelling that opened heaven and laid the earth. From then on the Way of Dharma flowed east. Huiyuan's Lotus Society, Sengyuan's rattan bed, the Fifth Patriarch's breaking of his head, old Lu's hunting band, Yinshan of the Western River, Shishuang's withered tree: among all whose names are recorded in the Transmission of the Lamp and listed in the histories of eminent monks, there is not one who did not come forth from deep mountains and lonely valleys in bitter emptiness and solitude. Alas, the world declines and the Way wanes, and people's hearts are not as of old. All who lodge their traces in the empty gate and place their form in the robe never fail to use me to steal a little ease, never knowing what leaving home is really about. They think the four offerings are theirs by right to enjoy, and do not reflect that the great matter of birth and death is the first task of one who has left home. The ancients left home solely for the one matter of birth and death: they called on teachers and visited friends, clarified their own affair, and then in deep mountains and lonely valleys, clothed in grass and eating from trees, propped up a broken-legged cauldron and cooked husked rice, sweeping and washing away all the shadows of former karmic consciousness without leaving a thread, and single-mindedly holding to the upward road, body like a withered tree, mind like cold ashes, until great enlightenment came and only then stopping. Only such a one may be called a true son of the Buddha and can repay the Buddha's deep grace. Chan monk, you have now brought forth a great and courageous mind and set your will on dwelling in the mountains. You need only put down all conditions, make your mind like a wall, raise one thought alone, and wish to equal the ancients, making the clarification of the great matter of birth and death your term: not clear, not stopping. Never imitate the people of the age who plan for stolen ease and make it provision for laziness. Go now, be my forerunner: clear the thatch on the slopes of Nanyue, and wait for this old man to finish repaying his debts and pass his remaining years there. Bear it in mind.
Instructions for the Chan monk Niansong Tong

Long ago Chan Master Zhongfeng dwelt at Tianmu. He had studied long under Gaofeng but his great matter was not yet clear, so he stood on a cliff edge holding a lone pine, and after seven days he was greatly enlightened. Even now that cliff pine stands alone, but those who follow in Zhongfeng's tracks are few indeed. The Chan monk Tong went to below that pine, cleared the thatch and built a hut, and dwelt there three years, reciting the Avatamsaka daily as his occupation. His diligence and austerity were certainly there, and his term far exceeded Zhongfeng's; yet as for clarifying that matter, he had not done it. Chan Master Daguan gave him the style Niansong, Remember the Pine, wishing him not to forget his origin. Now the Chan monk has come from afar to question me in the land of miasma, and is taking his leave of me: he will wander east past Zhiti, then go north into Wutai to seek Manjushri, hoping to find a companion among the ten thousand attendants, and beside the Vajra Cave recite the Avatamsaka a full hundred times to finish out his remaining years. On the point of setting out he begged a single phrase as the essential of the Dharma. I stroked my beard and laughed, saying: For you to hold this view is like crossing the sea to look for a river to bathe in. To enter the vast dharma-realm with narrow and shabby habits will be difficult. The ancients said: The whole great earth is one scroll of scripture; the whole great earth is the single eye of the monk. With such an eye reading such a scripture, to the end of the future there is never a moment of rest; what then of marks of coming and going, of views of this and that? The Avatamsaka takes the equal dharma-realm as its doctrine and non-obstruction as its gate. If one can awaken to this doctrine and enter this gate, then there is no thing that does not spread the body of Vairocana, no sound that does not proclaim the perfect wondrous tone, no moment in which one does not practice the conduct of Samantabhadra, and no person who is not a teacher numerous as dust motes. Then the samadhi of the net of light is clearly before the eyes, and the true scripture of universal eyes is complete with every thought; every step taken never leaves the field of stillness and extinction, and dwelling in the dust yet transcending it, one reaches at once the shore of prajna. Where then will you go to find Wutai, and by what dharma will you make the great sutra? Hence it is said: I wish to flee it, but cannot flee; beyond the great square all is filled up. If you can settle it in the present thought, why must you climb mountains and wade streams, seek companions, and recite words to finish out your remaining years? If you understand that birth is fundamentally unborn, then you abide nowhere. If you can awaken to the purport of non-abiding, you will naturally not give rise to thoughts of coming and going, movement and stillness, arising and ceasing. With the single phrase of the Sixth Patriarch, producing a mind that dwells nowhere, he cast off the inverted views of a hundred thousand ten thousand kalpas. You should here lift your eyebrows and look on high, and on no account stumble at the first step out the door and enter wholly into the wild grass.
Instructions for the Chief Seat Qian of Foling, Who Wrote Out the Avatamsaka Sutra in His Own Blood

Long ago I dwelt in the Nalaoyan cave by the Eastern Sea, and the Chan monk came from Wutai to visit me. When I crossed the mountains to Wuyang, he came again from Mount Kuang to comfort me in the land of miasma. Seeing him was like seeing kin from another life, and so I saw how human life is a dream. Among the disciples who came, we spent the summer retreat among the earthen ramparts, and on the day the retreat ended, Qian bowed and said: I will return to Donglin to follow in the fragrant footsteps of Huiyuan and imitate the pure practice of the Lotus Society, and I vow to prick my blood and write out the great Avatamsaka Sutra by hand, as pure karma adorning the Buddha-land. I beg one word of instruction. I said: Son of the Buddha, listen well. What do you take as the great sutra, and what as pure karma? Do you take the paper and ink you write on as the sutra, or the words and letters? Do you take movement and turning as pure karma, or the distribution of dots and strokes? If you take the paper and ink you write on as the sutra, then the documents in the marketplace are all the great sutra. If you take words and letters as the sutra, then talk, shouts, and joking worldly writing are all wondrous principle. In that case there is fundamentally nothing lacking, and why bother to write? If you take movement and turning as pure karma, then the everyday coughing, spitting, and swinging of the arm are nothing but Guanyin's perfect penetration by entering the principle. If you take the distribution of dots and strokes as pure karma, then greeting guests and entertaining visitors, lifting chopsticks and raising the spoon, are nothing but the wondrous conduct of Samantabhadra. If so, it is complete in itself, and why seek elsewhere? To set this aside and speak of a practice of dharma is like knowing two and five but not ten. Yet though all ten directions are the eternal stillness and light, fundamentally without brightness or darkness, and the whole dharma-realm is the pure land, fundamentally without coarse or fine; though the teeming myriad forms are all the spiritual text of the ocean-seal, and creatures with scales, shells, feathers, and fur are all the true body of the dharma-body; though the gibbon's cry and the bird's call all speak the perfect tone of non-duality, and rain falling and clouds moving fully reveal the wondrous function of spiritual power: if so, there is no turning away or toward, no coming or going, no grasping or rejecting, no beginning or end. The three times are thereby unchanged, and the ten ages are perfected in a single thought. This is the inexhaustible treasury of the dharma-realm. If within the inexhaustible treasury you wish, with a petty mind of arising and ceasing, to point to adornment of form and mark as the practice of dharma, and to seek the true cause of the Pure Land, that is to take cow dung for sandalwood and a fish eye for the wish-fulfilling jewel. Moreover, the single-character Dharma gate cannot be written out even with the sea for ink; yet you wish, with your limited four elements, your drop of blood, and your flash of time, to write out the inexhaustible true sutra and perform an inconceivable Buddha-work: this is like dotting and dyeing empty space, or grasping at lightning. Consider it. If not, then go to the peak of the Five Elders and look closely at the colors of the mountain and the light of the lake, and listen to the speech of birds and the sound of the stream, and ask what difference there is between this and the Vairocana Buddha sitting in the hall of universal light and, with bodies of cloud inexhaustible in the ten directions and an ocean-assembly of dust-mote lands, expounding the dharma-realm universally illuminating sutra. Investigate, investigate.
Instructions for the Chan monk Huaiyu Xiu

The student Tuxiu came from Wu with a single bowl and walked to the land of miasma, serving me for more than two years. I performed Buddha-work in the field of spears and halberds, and Xiu held his single thought with purity, putting work before the assembly and never tiring day or night, one day the same as the first. I often watched him from the cold corner of my eye, and he had no small air of a monk about him. Reflecting that in the final age those who take up this matter under the robe are hard to find, I loved him greatly in my heart. Lately he has taken leave of me to go and call on teachers in various places, and at the point of setting out he asked: The four elements are fundamentally empty and the five aggregates do not exist; where then is the illness? The old man said: The illness is in the place where there is no place. So I spoke this verse to aid his pilgrimage: The four elements are empty, and emptiness itself is the ill; the five aggregates do not exist, and existence is the fault. Cut off both ends and there is no news at all: then you will believe the family mountain is reached wherever you go.
Instructions for the Layman Xiqiao (a man of Jishui)

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: In all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts; yet toward deluded minds, do not suppress them either. Dwelling in states of deluded thought, do not add understanding; and toward no-understanding, do not discriminate the true. The ancients constantly took up these words to show students, but most fell into the nest of thinking. Only Zhongfeng annotated each one with the word no. This is the vajra ring.
Instructions for the Student Chen Zifu (a man of Jishui)

Confucius said: To know the incipient is divine indeed. The commentators say the incipient is the subtlety of movement; the student should fix his eye on the time before movement, and only then will he gain power.

When joy, anger, sorrow, and delight have not yet arisen, this is called the center. This is exactly the same as the Sixth Patriarch's not thinking of good and not thinking of evil: what is the original face of the Venerable? Investigate.

Writing is the patterning of the mind. Students who do not understand the substance of mind force stale phrases together; can that be called writing? It must flow out from one's own breast, and only then will it cover heaven and earth.
Mencius said: Food and sex are nature. These words seem like a footnote to the seventeen hundred cases; they are certainly not something a maker of chapters and sentences can understand.

The ancients said: The work lies in daily life. This is a dead phrase. To sit today in the nest of these words, even a person of resolve merely shows off the shadows of the conscious spirit. It is not the fault of the speaker, but of clinging to the words.

The Zongjing Lu says: In sound, one hears completely; outside seeing, there is no dharma. Whoever has not burst out and walked upon the crown of Vairocana's head will certainly not know where the huatou lands.

When a Confucian scholar has his will set on the Way, he seeks to do the work only within Chan; yet he does not know that holding it in mind and resting in it is itself the first ground of the supreme vehicle.

When the night breath is clear and bright, gather the mind and sit upright; turn the gaze inward and illuminate within, and in the still and undimmed place you will see your own original face. Do not deceive yourself. Confucius said: I have not seen one who loves virtue as he loves beauty. That is enough to know that those in the world who do not deceive themselves are few.
A whirlwind and a sudden rain come sighing down: try to observe where the wind comes from and where the rain arrives from. If you can see this clearly, the ten thousand things are within you.

It is like fine sprouts that one hopes will flower and bear grain: if the grubs and pests are not removed, it is hard for them to ripen. This is so not only in the world, but in the monastery for those who study the Way as well.
Instructions for the Chan monk Liji Zhao

As for this matter, there is fundamentally no upward and no downward; as soon as thinking is involved it becomes leftover dharma, much less when one enters the reality beyond words with a mind that seeks to gain something. Chan monk, if you can truly resolve that birth and death are the great matter, then try this: take all your former thoughts of wearying of the world, and everything you have seen, heard, and understood since leaving home, and the daily work you have applied in seeking your original portion, dressing and eating, turning and bowing, looking up, moving and resting, busy and at leisure, and all the states before you that you have passed through, and investigate them minutely: what after all do you take as the upward matter? Then take the mind that investigates and observe it truly: where after all does it land? Wherever there is a landing place, it becomes a nest; that is the cave of birth and death, all matters on the side of deluded thought, not reality. The sutra says: Even if you extinguish all seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, and keep guard within over the quiet and idle, this is still a shadow matter of discriminating the dust of dharmas. The ancients called it the black mountain and the ghost cave; it is precisely the great taboo in Chan practice. How much less can one enter the ultimate with a mind of arising and ceasing and coarse floating imagination. It is far, far away. As it is said, to raise the mind is already to err; to move a thought is already to depart. If you take not raising the mind and not moving a thought as the mysterious and wondrous, you fall again into the nest of the mysterious and wondrous. A monk asked Zhaozhou: What is the mystery within mystery? Zhou said: How long have you been mystifying? The monk said: A long time. Zhou said: Were it not for this old monk, you would have been mystified to death. See how one phrase of the ancients is like the vajra king's sword, cutting off all the views of sages and ordinary beings. Seen thus, how could this matter be spoken by the lips, or described in paper, ink, and letters? It lies only in the student's daily life, at the place where the mind arises and moves, truly observing. So long as the least trace of feeling or view, or any mysterious and wondrous understanding, sticks fast anywhere, it is a shadow of deluded thought and falls to the edge of birth and death; it is not detachment from the boundary. The boundary of detachment from the boundary is called reality. Reality has no boundary; having no boundary, it does not fall to the boundary of sages and ordinary beings. Sages and ordinary beings do not fall, and the feeling of birth and death is finished. What the ancients called one thought not arising, the boundary of before and after cut off: cut off, and there is nothing to do. Then one is named a person of the Way with nothing to do. Since affairs are already nothing, where would you seek the mysterious and the wondrous? As it is said: Simply exhaust ordinary feeling; there is no other sagely understanding. Reaching here, it is like a person drinking water, knowing for himself whether it is cold or warm, much like a mute eating yellow cedar: hard to disclose to anyone. Chan monk, only prepare a heart and guts of raw iron and go on straight like this. Do not use the mind to wait for awakening, and do not count the years, months, and days; you need only take the measureless kalpas of before and after and lift them directly into the present. Let birth and death come and go, arise and cease as they will; this one present thought is decisive and will not be moved by any floating light or phantom shadow. Even if it be a mountain of knives or a blaze of fire, a Pure Land or a heavenly palace, let them rise and sink as they will; this single thought of lone light will after all not be shaken or snatched away. Such a one may be called a person of great strength, and only then is he a true one who has left home, not enveloped by birth and death, not buried by sages and ordinary beings, not shifted by the three times. Only thus are name and reality in accord, and this is true detachment from the boundary. Chan monk, take these words and ask the clear-eyed teachers of every quarter to confirm them, and on no account take them as Chan Way or Buddhadharma.
Instructions for the Hall Master Huaiyu Xiu

The ancients said: The whole ten-direction world is entirely the single eye of the monk; the empty space and the myriad forms, creatures with scales, shells, feathers, and fur, the vast and the minute, the huge and the tiny, are entirely the single scroll of the great Vairocana canon. With such an eye reading such a scripture, to the end of the future one never rests and never ceases. This is the least and most minute fraction of Buddha-work within a single pore of the great being Samantabhadra. One hair is thus; how much more every pore? The pores of the direct retribution are thus; how much more the dust motes of the worlds of dependent retribution? One dust mote is thus; how much more every dust mote? And a dust mote contains vast lands; how much more the lands of every dust mote and the dust of every land? Contemplating deeply thus, the boundless ocean of lands does not separate self and other by a hairsbreadth, and the ten ages and ancient and modern never depart from the present thought in beginning or end. This is the true scripture of Samantabhadra. To be able to see this scripture is to have the wisdom eye of Manjushri. With this eye, look at the beings within the dust: every being fully expounds this scripture, and everyone who hears it understands at once that all sages and ordinary beings are fundamentally without two and without difference. We ourselves possess this eye, turn this scripture, and deliver these beings; though it be said that one exhausts the great compassion and fulfills the great vow through dust-mote kalpas, there is no weariness at all. Yet even so, it is not the monk's own portion. Why? Because in the pure dharma-realm there is fundamentally no shaking or coming and going, no images of sages and ordinary beings. Since even this supreme image does not exist, how much less the various deluded views, the Buddhadharma and Chan Way, and all the inverted marks of grasping and rejecting, which are vain shadows? Thus we know that the Buddhas and patriarchs from of old showed people only how to rest the mad mind and not to seek from another. As it is said: Just untie the soiled robe from your own breast; why labor to boast of diligence abroad? It is also said: Simply exhaust ordinary feeling; there is no other sagely understanding. If you make a sagely understanding, you fall into a crowd of wrong views. All the spiritual powers above are the original portion and nothing extraordinary; this one flavor of the ordinary, why seek any other Buddhadharma?
Instructions for the Chan monk Liaoji (bing-wu year)

When I restored Caoxi and rebuilt the Baolin Chan Hall to receive those who came from the four directions, the Chan monk Liang made a vow to beg for alms to support the assembly. At the start of the summer retreat, the Chan monk offered incense and asked for instruction, and I therefore instructed him, saying: The wondrous practices by which the Buddhas benefit beings are not of one kind, and the wondrous gates by which bodhisattvas become Buddha are not of one road. Long ago the great being Vimalakirti performed Buddha-work with a single bowl of rice: thirty-two thousand beings of measurable number ate that food and all entered the discipline of practice. Tell me, since the bowl remains as of old and the fragrant rice is as usual, where is the discipline of those who eat it, and where is the spiritual power of the one who brought the rice? If you see through this, it is exactly what is meant by those who are equal in food being equal in dharma. If you cannot see through, you must call on teachers, resolve your doubts, and only when you reach the place of no doubt will you accord in some small measure with your original ground. Otherwise you will inevitably drift with the waves. That is why when a monk came to Zhaozhou and said, The student has just entered the monastery; I beg the Master to instruct me, Zhou said, Have you eaten your gruel? The monk said, I have. Zhou said, Then wash your bowl. And the monk had an insight. Chan monk, if you can understand where Zhaozhou spoke and where that monk had his insight, then you will walk arm in arm with all the good people in Vimalakirti's chamber.
The Dream Wanderings Collection of Old Man Hanshan, Volume Four
Instructions for the Layman Rongyu (jia-chen year)

When I was living at the Sanyi Hut in Leiyang, the layman Wang Rongyu of Huazhou asked: Your disciple has long turned his heart to the Way, but his resolve is not yet single. I think that since birth I have been taught by the names of the sages and take loyalty and filial piety as first; I am ashamed that I have not won fame and rank to be loyal to my ruler, nor earned a small salary to be filial to my parents. My heart is not at ease, and so it is hard to settle my resolve. I said: So it is. Loyalty and filial piety are the substance of the great Way and the goodness of the human heart. How could there be a Way that abandons loyalty and filial piety, or a practice that turns its back on mind and nature? The world's Confucians lump our Buddha's teaching together and say it abandons human relations and casts off loyalty and filial piety, and so is at odds with them; they do not understand that what it turns its back on is the trace, and what it turns toward is the mind. The Records say: To think of serving one's parents, one cannot but know others; to think of knowing others, one cannot but know heaven. The human is humaneness, the virtue of nature. From this we see that to discuss serving one's parents without knowing others is not to be called filial; to discuss knowing others without knowing heaven is not to be called knowing others; and to speak of knowing heaven without seeing one's nature leaves heaven itself vague and without ground. Thus mind and nature are in oneself, and are the natural heavenly truth. To know the truth of the heavenly nature is to be a true person; to practice the filial piety of the heavenly truth is to be a true filial son. To cultivate oneself by the work of seeing one's nature is true cultivation; to delight one's parents with the joy of the truth of nature is wondrous practice. To be filial in this way is the utmost of filial piety. To say meanly that reverence is weighty while food and clothing are light is even more petty. Yu said: Your disciple receives your clear instruction. The work of seeing one's nature is indeed great, and to delight my parents thereby is truly what I wish. But it is like gazing at the ocean: vast and without a guide. I beg the Master to point out a shortcut. I said: The ancients said: There is only the shortcut of practice: simply recite Amitabha Buddha. Amitabha in Sanskrit is rendered as Measureless Life; Buddha means awakened. It is our own natural, heavenly awakened nature, and the first wondrous gate for seeing one's nature. This nature, before heaven and earth, does not grow old; after heaven and earth, it does not end. Birth and death do not change it; change and succession do not shift it. It transcends the ten thousand things and has no end; therefore it is called Measureless Life. This life does not belong to the body's length or shortness, or to the stretching out or shortening of years. If we can see this nature, we are named Buddha. And Buddha is not the title of a sage in the West; it is the truth of our own nature. Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang were the first among heaven's people to awaken. Heaven's people await something and can then awaken; the sages were born awakened first. Is this awakening not the awakening of Buddha-nature? What Mencius meant by Yao and Shun being the same as other people is this. If one can awaken to this nature, then everyone can be a Yao or a Shun; and since everyone can be a Yao or a Shun, it is clear that everyone can become Buddha. Alas, people of the world are bound by narrow, one-sided views and have not met the teaching of a true person; they are tied by vulgar learning and take hearsay for the highest truth. No wonder they are vague and do not know where to return. Yu said: By your instruction, disciple, I believe and know that the mind itself is Buddha and that the mind itself makes Buddha, without seeking outside. But I do not know the purport of making Buddha, or the work to begin with. I beg you to teach me. I said: If we know that our own mind is Buddha, we should examine why we have become sentient beings. For sentient beings and Buddha are like water and ice: when the mind is deluded, Buddha becomes a sentient being; when the mind awakens, the sentient being is Buddha. It is like water becoming ice and ice melting into water: the name changes, not the substance. Deluded, one is not awake; not awake, one is a sentient being. Not deluded, one is awake; awake, the sentient being is Buddha. If you wish to seek Buddha, seek only your own mind. If the mind is deluded, you need only recite the Buddha; when the Buddha is raised, one is awake, and being awake, the light of self-nature stands forth alone. Former deluded thoughts, greed, anger, and delusion, melt at once like ice. Once karmic grime is dissolved, the mind is pure and utterly free of burden. Where there is nothing, suffering goes and joy remains, calamity goes and blessing remains. Once true joy remains, there is no nature in which one is not joyful; when heavenly blessing appears, there is no circumstance in which one is not at peace. Only this true peace and utmost joy: how could the mouth and body bring it, or wealth and rank reach it? This is what is meant by when the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure. The work of the mind is no other than this, and the provision for the Pure Land is no other than this. Yu said: Hearing the teaching, my mind and eyes are opened, as if I saw the road home, with no doubt remaining. But how does reciting the Buddha amount to filial piety? This is what is not yet at ease; I beg the Master to instruct me. I said: Long ago a filial son went far away. A guest came to his mother, who looked for her son and he did not return, so she bit her finger, and the son's heart ached at once; knowing his mother was thinking of him, he turned back home at once. The mother bit her finger and the son's heart ached because their bodies were one and their minds one. If you can clearly see your own mind and suddenly awaken to the fact that your own mind is your mother's mind, then with your own awakening awaken your mother, and with your own mindfulness wish your mother mindful. Since a mother loves her son's form, would she not love her son's mind? If a mother loves her son's form, then the form is a burden and the mind suffers; if a mother loves her son's mind, then the form is forgotten and the mind is joyful. Moreover, mother and son are one in the substance of mind. Formerly the mother thought of her son and, biting her finger, the son's heart ached; now the son thinks of his mother and forgets form, and would the mother's mind not be at peace and joyful? I fear only that your work of the mind is not earnest enough and your study of forgetting form not deep enough, so that you cannot match the urgency of your mother's thought of you and gladden her heart. Therefore the filial sons of old did not exchange the care of five cauldrons and three victims for the joy of playing in a spotted robe before their parents. The greatness of filial piety lies in delighting the parents' minds, not in nourishing their forms. Such is worldly filial piety. If you can make your mother's remaining years turn her heart from now on toward the Pure Land and enjoy a single day's happiness, that surpasses a hundred years of wealth and rank, which only leaves her nursing a sorrowful heart. For although another may have wealth and rank, if the parent is not happy, then even in joy there is something that makes for unhappiness. Now you, by reciting the Buddha, can make your mother's mind at peace and joyful, joyful and lasting: is this not Measureless Life? If the mother's life is measureless, the son's life is measureless too. So the Pure Land is in oneself and not in another; the Buddha is in the mind and not in traces. Set your will on this.
Instructions for the Chan monk Zian You on Dwelling in the Mountains

The Buddha said that all sentient beings wander in birth and death, and that deluded inversion is the root of it all. When the inverted thought is extinguished and one willingly consents in one's own heart, that is the hour of ending birth and death and escaping the sea of suffering. If deluded thoughts do not rest, birth and death are hard to escape. Hence it is said: If the mad mind does not rest, when it rests, that is bodhi. If we can truly rest the mad mind at once, then we have left the three realms, broken the army of Mara, and sit in the open ground, called a person of the Way with nothing to do. Though old man Yama of the iron face have a ruthless heart and poisonous hands, he has no way to scheme or grope for you. Coming and going at will, free and at ease: a greatly liberated person. At such an hour, even to call one a Buddha or a patriarch would be unbearable to hear; how much less would one be willing to go into a latrine and herd with stupid flies, stealing stench and pouncing on filth. The ten directions all become the Pure Land, and with the great perfect enlightenment as my monastery, body and mind fill it, and I walk arm in arm with all the Buddhas of the ten directions, gaining great freedom. Then the hut is the self and the self is the hut; the hut is the mountain and the mountain is the person. No inside, no outside, no other, no this. Thus one dwells where there is no dwelling, walks where there is no walking, cultivates where there is no cultivating, and only then is it called one's own hut. If instead one nurtures laziness and sleeps stupidly, then for three lives and sixty kalpas one is only a servant for others. Think it over, think it over.
Instructions for the Chan monk Qingyun

One who has left home must clarify the great matter. First, he must have a genuine and urgent mind for birth and death. Second, he must bring forth a decisive resolve to leave birth and death. Third, he must stake his whole life on an integrity that does not change until death. Fourth, he must truly know that the world is suffering and give rise to the utmost weariness and detachment. Fifth, he must draw near to the supreme teacher and be endowed with right views, constantly asking for instruction, obeying and following the teaching, and practicing as taught with diligence and without slackness; not blocked by the five desires and afflictions, not driven by evil habits, not moved by evil friends, not robbed by evil conditions, and not discouraged by his own dull faculties. Bringing forth the mind thus and advancing thus, after long familiarity it will naturally fit his original vow like box and lid. Even if in this life he cannot awaken and clearly see his own mind, then through a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives, today will still be his first causal ground. If not, and he merely uses narrow and base views, soft and warm habits, and drifting ease, and with lip-Chan, a wild mind, a turbid spirit, and the root of wrong views takes these as the proper business of one who has left home, and with this hopes to escape the sea of suffering, it is like going to Yue by way of Yan, or stepping backward and seeking to go forward. Alas, alas, in the final age those of right faith are few. Chan monk, since you know your direction, you should clearly know your own mind and make truth and decisiveness the foremost meaning. Strive on, strive on.
Instructions for the Chan monk Ruchang

The Buddha said: To take leave of one's parents and leave home, to know the mind and reach the root, to understand the unconditioned Dharma, this is called a shramana, always practicing the two hundred and fifty precepts. He also said: To cut off desire and put away craving, to know the source of one's own mind, to reach the Buddha's profound principle, to awaken to the unconditioned Dharma. And again: To shave head and beard and become a shramana, to receive the Buddhadharma, to put away worldly goods, to be content with what is begged, eating once a day and lodging one night beneath a tree, careful never to do so twice. What makes people foolish and dull is love and desire. In such teachings he admonished with every kind of earnest and bitter word, all for the sake of those who are disciples of the Buddha: that at the very first, leaving home, they should make the leaving of desire their first practice.
