The descendants of later ages, though they leave home in body, are drunk in heart with the five desires, and do not know what affliction is the dharma of detachment, or what road is the road out of suffering. Tangled and confused, they do not wake of themselves; and further they counterfeit dignity and pretend to virtue, deceiving others outwardly and their own minds inwardly, harboring flaws without knowing it. To seek one of true mind and right mindfulness is hard to find. Vimalakirti said: The straightforward mind is the place of practice. Ruchang, since you have the will to seek the dharma of detachment, you should make the straightforward mind the foremost meaning. Take care.
Instructions for My Young Master Dezong

Since you began to follow this old man, more than twenty years have passed, and not only have you labored in your duties; you have also met with calamity and walked the land of miasma, and that three times now. Earlier I sent you back to the mountain home to serve your teacher, but your mad mind did not rest and you came back to me. Now I hear that your teacher has become a thing of the past, and you were unable to hold his towel and vase while he lived, or to lift his hands and feet when he died. Can you be called his disciple? You are going back now; do you not think how you will repay your teacher's grace in the unseen? The ancients called on teachers and visited friends precisely to accomplish the work of the Way. You have followed your teacher more than twenty years: where is your work of the Way? The ancients were ashamed to face their parents, teachers, and friends; since your work of the Way is not accomplished, fortunately you have no parents, teachers, or friends left, so you have no place to put your shame. The patriarch said: Sentient beings are no different from Buddha; it is only that sentient beings have many habits and the Buddhas and patriarchs are pure and stainless. You have served a good spiritual friend and heard his instructions with your own ears, and you are old now, yet you are still so drifting. Do you not know how, in the days to come, you will face this old monk? If by any chance this old monk were like your parents, I fear you would have no place to put your shame in this life either. I think of your loyal heart and righteous courage, which are not less than the ancients'. Yesterday I read the words of the great master Daguan, who compared you to Tian Guang. If so, how shall this old monk repay you for your life? It is said that among all offerings the Dharma is foremost. Now I make this a further offering to repay your life. Never again forget the words of today's parting. At the fork in the road I hold your hand and urge you earnestly: take care.
Instructions for the Attendant Hui

The Buddha appeared in the world for the sake of one great cause: to lead beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter the Buddha's knowledge and vision. Yet the Buddha's knowledge and vision are the knowledge and vision of sentient beings, and the knowledge and vision of sentient beings are the knowledge and vision of birth and death. Hence it is said: When knowledge and vision establish knowing, that is the root of ignorance; when knowledge and vision are without seeing, that is nirvana. Thus the knowledge and vision of sages and ordinary beings are not two, and the difference of delusion and awakening lies only in whether one establishes or not. The patriarch said: If you establish a single dust mote, the country is destroyed and the family perishes. For knowledge and vision are fundamentally without sage or ordinary; but wherever there is establishment, there is a self, and where there is a self all obstacles arise at once; where there is no self, the ten thousand dharmas sink level. Thus we know that the self is the root of birth and death. Not only do ordinary people make greed, anger, and delusion and so become obstructed by self; even all the sages and cultivators, so long as their knowledge and vision are not forgotten, are entirely obstructed by self, and this is the root of birth and death that is hardest to pull out. Therefore among the two kinds of obstacle there is coarse and fine: the coarse is easy to dismiss, the fine hard to remove. Because knowledge and vision are deeply hidden and rooted in the mind, they are hard to pull out. Hence the sutra says: To preserve the self and to be aware of the self are both called obstacles. This is precisely the knowledge and vision establishing knowing, hidden as deeply as life itself, which one cannot cut off oneself. That is why the ancients spent twenty or thirty years in bitter study; and even if one awakens to the fact that one's own nature is complete, like the bright moon over a cold pool or the sound of a bell in the still night, undiminished however it is struck and undispersed however the waves touch it, this is still a matter on the shore of birth and death. This is where the ancients greatly did not deceive themselves; for to deceive oneself and others is to destroy oneself and others. The attendant Fuhui left home with this old man early. When I first saw him he was a dull lump; after ten years away he came back duller still. Yet I have always been glad that within his dullness there is a wakeful undull place. This attendant makes this dull-and-not-dull his root of life. Now five more years have passed; his dullness increases daily, and his undull part too grows secretly and silently. Thus people look at the attendant and see dullness, and the attendant looks at himself and sees himself duller still; but no one knows his own dullness. This summer the old man returned to the mountain from western Yue, and the attendant suddenly put on his dull look, and the old man laughed aloud: his dullness will never have its day. I said privately that this dull man makes dullness his own fault. If he can take this dullness as his own place of use, he will be quite content, and can end birth and death, and will not betray the matter of leaving home and wandering. But if he further establishes this dullness, then the illness is worse than knowledge and vision establishing knowing. Attendant, if you can push over this dullness, you need not worry that your eyebrows will not be tied together with this old man's.
Instructions for Deng Sizhi

The Buddhas and patriarchs appeared in the world and taught the dharma of prajna, teaching people to cultivate with prajna as the root. Prajna is Sanskrit; in Chinese it means wisdom. This wisdom is the Buddha-nature inherent in us, also called one's own mind, also called self-nature. This substance is fundamentally undefiled, therefore it is called pure; fundamentally undimmed, therefore it is called luminous; fundamentally vast and all-embracing, therefore it is called empty space; fundamentally without delusion, therefore it is called one truth; fundamentally unmoving and unchanging, therefore it is called true suchness, also called thusness; fundamentally perfect and illuminating all, therefore it is called perfect enlightenment; fundamentally still and extinguished, therefore it is called nirvana. In the Buddhas it is perfectly realized, and so is called great enlightenment, also called bodhi. The Buddhas use it, and so it is the wondrous function of spiritual power; bodhisattvas cultivate it, and it is named wondrous practice; the two vehicles attain it, and it is named liberation; ordinary people are deluded about it, and it becomes deluded thought and karmic consciousness. When it is aroused and used, it becomes greed, anger, delusion, craving, pride, flattery, and deceit; when it is made into karma, it becomes lust, killing, theft, and lying; and the fruit it reaps is knives, saws, iron, grindstones, and even cauldrons of boiling water and furnaces of coals, all kinds of instruments of suffering, all transformed from this mind. It is just like a waking man at ease, with all kinds of joyful states before his eyes; after a little while he falls into a heavy sleep and suddenly dreams he is in hell, where all the instruments of suffering and their agonies are borne at once, unbearable and unendurable, and just when he seeks help and cannot get it, the guests chatting in the hall outside have not yet fallen silent, and he wakes with a start, moaning as he rises. He looks and the scene of joy is still before his eyes, the wine still warm and the dishes still hot; the place on the pillow and mat has not been left, yet the states of suffering and joy are suddenly different. In short, joy comes from outside, suffering comes from within. From this we see that the doctrine of heaven and hell appears plainly within one's own mind; how could it be a mere phantom marvel? It is all just where one's own deluded mind has arrived. The sutra says: The mind takes what is of the mind, and the unreal becomes unreal dharma. It also says: The dharmas above and below in the three realms are made by one mind alone. Seen thus, it is not the Buddhadharma alone that teaches one mind; from the sages and worthies of old down to all the nine schools and strange arts, to speak at the utmost, even to sentient and insentient things, none is not established from this one mind. Only there is difference of great and small, many and few, good and evil, right and wrong, bright and dim, and the use each makes is different. Hence it is said: Mountains, rivers, and the great earth fully reveal the body of the Dharma King; creatures with scales, shells, feathers, and fur universally manifest the samadhi of the body of form. All this is the true light of prajna and the shadow matter of our own mind. The substance of mind inherent in us is thus vast, all-embracing, pure, and luminous; and the various states and forms of things that lie crossed and crowded around us are thus all manifested by our own mind. That we have this and do not know it is indeed pitiable. And worse, we mistake what comes from our own mind and take it as the happy ground of craving and love: the eye delights in beautiful forms, the ear in licentious sounds, the nose in scents, the tongue in flavors, the body in touches, and the mind in dharmas; and all these too come forth from our own mind. We take them further and make them joy, make them pleasure, make them greed, anger, and delusion, make them lust, killing, theft, and lying, and so make all kinds of illusory karma, and further invite the fierce suffering of the three evil paths in the future. It is like a man dreaming and not waking. Is this not greatly pitiable? Because this mind is one substance with all the Buddhas and not two, and because the patriarchs of every generation awakened to it and were no different from them, only we possess it fully and do not know it as illusion. The son ran away and forgot to return, and the parents thought of him and searched for him. That is why Shakyamuni appeared in the world, why Bodhidharma came from the west, and why what Caoxi taught for more than thirty years, and the seventeen hundred cases that flowed down to point people to, are all this matter. It is not old Lu alone: what this old man speaks to Sizhi today is also this matter; and what Sizhi and all those present who hear and see it share is also this matter. The sutra says: This is the one and only matter; the other two are not true. Thus we know that apart from this one matter, everything becomes the talk of Mara and idle discourse. If the Buddhas, who have fully realized it, did not appear in the world, they would fail sentient beings; if the patriarchs, who awakened to it, did not teach the Dharma, they would fail the Buddhas; and whoever hears it but does not believe, understand, accept, and practice it fails himself. To fail sentient beings is arrogance; to fail the Buddhas is downfall; to fail oneself is folly. Thus the Buddhas and patriarchs may be failed, but oneself must not be failed, since one has it inherently and does not seek it, possesses it fully and does not make good use of it. It is like holding a pearl and begging: is this not greatly pitiable? Sizhi, you now bear a body in the sea of dust and your mind has fallen into a deluded road; suddenly you wake with a start and turn back to seek this matter, like the son holding the pearl who is ashamed to herd with beggars, and mind after mind asks people for the way to be self-sufficient. This old man at once points this dharma straight at you, as if showing you the divine pearl at the hem of your robe: it was Sizhi's own all along, and it is not this old man handing it to you as a favor or a worldly courtesy. Yet this wish-fulfilling jewel responds to every request, and all kinds of undertakings and states of use are fully supplied by it. As for the way to make it respond as you wish, that again lies in Sizhi's own mind, in your skill, diligence, and strenuous effort. If you can truly consent and strive with all your might, and one day suddenly awaken, then you will swallow in a single mouthful the mountains, rivers, and great earth, creatures with scales, shells, feathers, and fur, the Buddhas of the three times, the patriarchs of every generation, and the undertakings of Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius, without borrowing another's strength. Otherwise you remain a sentient being of dream inversion; how then could you be called a true man? Sizhi, Sizhi, better to fail the Buddhas and patriarchs above and this old man below than ever to fail yourself, your ruler, or your parents. The prajna this old man speaks today is all the mind-ground Dharma gate of the Buddhas and patriarchs from of old, and it does not differ by a single character from what the Sixth Patriarch first taught. Only, of those who first heard it, you are the only one. Since one man now stands in place of the twelve hundred of old, this old man cannot contain his joy, and so he too teaches the dharma of prajna. As our Buddha and patriarchs said: as for one person, so for the many. If Deng holds this to benefit self and others, it may well become a broad and long tongue.
Instructions for the Chan monk Miaoguang Miao

The conditions for entering the Way and the roads into it differ for each. Following the prajna seed-nature of former habits, they are shallow or deep and not the same. Some first cast aside letters and simply raise the huatou of an ancient's karmic condition, and so awaken and enter. Some first study the various wondrous gates of practice within the teachings, and afterwards throw away the mixed poisons and rely solely on contemplation to awaken and enter. Thus the great master Yongjia, through the Tiantai practice of stopping and seeing, suddenly saw his own mind as clearly as a fruit in the palm; and when he met Caoxi, he was like a lion slipped from its ropes, and old Lu, exhausting all his divine power, could only say, Just so, just so. This is the first model among the teachers from of old. The Chan monk Xuan has traveled everywhere and long relied on lecture halls, and has already glimpsed a part of the Buddha vehicle's teaching eye. If, from what he has glimpsed, he can cut away all views and the habits of letters, and apart from letters single-mindedly raise and thoroughly investigate the Buddha's and patriarchs' upward road, inquiring day and night until he reaches the place where the Buddha had not yet appeared and the patriarch had not yet come from the west, a single cold place, and suddenly it bursts forth from within his own breast like a bean popping in cold ashes: then he will believe that all dharmas do not go beyond his own mind, and that all the mountains, rivers, the great earth, blades of grass, motes of dust, and hairs are all himself. Then he may let things take their course and, as suits the occasion, perform the conditions of giving the Dharma. This is what is called opening the gate of sweet dew and walking upon the crown of the Buddhas' and patriarchs' heads. But if the mind and will are narrow and base, and one takes the leftover tea and cold rice of the lips as the supreme wondrous flavor, then one cannot even save oneself; how would one dare to speak of the knowledge and vision of Buddhadharma?
Instructions for the Pilgrim Kuan Liang

People of old went on pilgrimage for the sake of birth and death; people today merely go on pilgrimage and do not know birth and death. This is greatly to be pitied; this is what is meant by using it daily and not knowing it. The fault lies in not knowing what one originally has. If a person knows what he has, he knows to value himself; knowing to value himself, he does not follow things and can turn things instead. The Book of Songs says: My heart is not a stone; it cannot be turned. You must know that unless it is a vajra mind-ground, nothing fails to be turned by things. Once turned by things, one follows them along. Can such a one be called a pilgrim monk? Kuan Liang came from the north to the south and has come to comfort me several times, and has not been turned by the hardships of the road, hunger, and cold. This old man only knows that his heels are strong, and so called him Iron Foot. Now, seeing that his mind does not shift, I further praise him with the words Iron Guts. Yet iron guts are what this old man knows; the matter of his pilgrimage is certainly not what you know. If you knew a little about pilgrimage, you would not go straight on like that. This old man pities his foolishness and fears for what he does not know, and so sends him off with this letter. Go on pilgrimage again. If after this you still cannot grope for your own nostrils, then on some later day it will surely be hard to meet as we meet today.
Instructions for the Chan monk Ruliang

The Buddha said: To shave head and beard and become a novice, to be free of desire and still, is the foremost of all. Thus we know that desire is the first and greatest matter at the head of the road of birth and death. Therefore the Buddha sharply rebuked it and warned against it. Apart from it, one gains peace and happiness. The reason sentient beings sink in the sea of suffering and cannot quickly reach the other shore is solely that desire is the fault and the affliction. The Buddha said: The root of all suffering is craving; if craving is extinguished, there is nothing to rely on. The three realms are the house in which all beings take their stand, and desire is its foundation; the clamor and noise of the toils of the dust are all this. If one wants to leave that reliance at once, then there is no question of breaking the three poisons, leaving the three realms, and breaking the net of Mara; then the Tathagata is greatly delighted. Thus we know that if the five desires are not left behind, the three realms are hard to break; how sorrowful the Tathagata must be. To seek stillness and liberation is then difficult. Ruliang left home young and went on pilgrimage in many places; now he has met this old man, brought forth the bodhi mind, been given the novice precepts, and resolved to practice the conduct of detachment from desire. This is the first wondrous practice of one who vows to leave birth and death. I fear only that his resolve is not firm and his practice not strong. The Buddha said: One must long endure bitter effort before it can be accomplished. You should have a decisive resolve, and not stop until you become Buddha. This is the true resolve to practice the conduct of detachment from desire.
